id: how is python written_Python Execution Process_0
text: Why is Python considered slow? As it compiles and interprets code at runtime, unlike languages like C/C++ that compile directly to machine code.

id: how is python written_Python Execution Process_1
text: Most modern language interpreters are written in C, and Python's most popular implementation (CPython) is no exception.

id: how is python written_Python Execution Process_2
text: The Python execution process:

id: how is python written_Python Execution Process_3
text: 1. Python compiler reads source code 2. Code is saved as a `.py` file 3. Compilation stage: source code is converted to bytecode and a `.pyc` file is generated 4. Python Virtual Machine (PVM) interprets the bytecode 5. PVM converts bytecode to machine code (binary) 6. CPU executes the machine code for the final output

id: hello world of neural networks_Introduction_0
text: Think of how your brain learns new things.

id: hello world of neural networks_Introduction_1
text: How does your brain adapt to situations? That is essentially what we are trying to replicate with the computer when it comes to AI (for now)

id: hello world of neural networks_Introduction_2
text: This a long one. There are sections which yall losers who failed in 11th grade math like me can skip.

id: hello world of neural networks_Perceptron_0
text: The idea of neural networks originates from perceptrons used in the early 1950s. (Perceptron: https://i.ibb.co/MyYjM37N/perceptron.png)

id: hello world of neural networks_Perceptron_1
text: Networks composed of perceptrons where outputs from one layer feed into the next are called feedforward neural networks.

id: hello world of neural networks_Perceptron_2
text: While perceptrons were limited to linear decision boundaries, modern neural networks use multiple layers and non-linear activation functions to learn complex patterns.

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_0
text: *Given an image which with a handwritten number, how do you identify the number?*

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_1
text: It's simple for us because we've seen numbers all our lives. But how do *WE* identify them? Sure we've seen them all our lives but how does our brain see them?

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_2
text: We know what strokes 2's have, it has a little horizontal line as a base & a slight curved S shaped line. So it must be a 2.

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_3
text: **How can we make a computer learn this?**

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_4
text: *Visual Pattern Recognition* is a hard program to write on the computer if not for neural networks.

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_5
text: Simple intuitions about how we recognize shapes - **"a 9 has a loop at the top, and a vertical stroke in the bottom right"** - turn out to be not so simple to express to a computer.

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_6
text: When you try to make such rules precise it doesn't work.

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_7
text: Idea is:

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_8
text: - Take a large number of handwritten digits (training data) - Develop system that learns from this (infer rules for recognizing handwritten digits) - Test on new image and see how well it predicts.

id: hello world of neural networks_Problem Statement_9
text: Try to think about this in a smarter way.

id: hello world of neural networks_Framework_0
text: - Each image is *28 * 28* pixels (which can be represented as numbers) - Each of these pixels has a *weight* value attached to it which indicates how much those pixels matter. - *Example:* in a '2' only pixels containing horizontal line as a base and a S shaped curve pixels will matter, all other pixels are just dead weight. - Large values of weights indicates that it matters a lot. By varying the weights and the threshold, we can get different models of decision-making. - Somehow make sure all these images learn some underlying pattern and are able to recognise what the image is saying. - This happens via some trial and error, predicting some jargon at first (known as the *forward pass*) - Then hopefully minimising that error and making some sense out of it (known as the *backward pass*) - Given a new image, how well can the neural network predict what number this image is?

id: hello world of neural networks_Basics Revisited_0
text: - **Neuron**: Thing that holds a number between 0-1 i.e activation value (0-1, grayscale, white numbers : 1, black numbers : 0) - **Activation Functions**: Introduce non-linearity in data otherwise every data is just a bunch of matrix multiplications on other layers - *Examples:* Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU (more on these later, just think of them as math functions which transforms your data x into f(x)) - **Weights**: Determine the strength of connections. - **Biases**: Shift activations to improve flexibility.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias and Weights Explained**_0
text: Bias and weights are the building blocks of neural networks. Let’s break them down:

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias: The Intercept**_0
text: Bias is like the intercept in the equation of a line \(y = mx + c\). It shifts the output up or down, even when the inputs are zero. Without bias, the output is forced to be zero when all inputs are zero, which limits the flexibility of the model.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias: The Intercept**_1
text: Mathematically: $\text{output} = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + b$

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias: The Intercept**_2
text: Here, \(b\) (bias) ensures that the neuron’s “neutral” point can shift up or down, allowing the model to better fit the data.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias: The Intercept**_3
text: Think of bias as the constant $c$ in $y = mx + c$. Without $c$, all lines must pass through the origin (0, 0). With $c$, you can move the line up or down, giving the model more flexibility.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias: The Intercept**_4
text: Without bias, zero input forces zero output.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Bias: The Intercept**_5
text: Bias is just a number added all the time, even when the inputs are zero, so the neuron’s “neutral” point can shift up or down.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Weights: The Slope**_0
text: Weights determine the strength of the connection between inputs and outputs. They act like the slope \(m\) in \(y = mx + c\), controlling how much influence each input $x_i$ has on the output.

id: hello world of neural networks_**Weights: The Slope**_1
text: Large weights amplify the importance of certain inputs, while small weights reduce their impact. By adjusting weights during training, the model learns which inputs matter most for making accurate predictions.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_0
text: - Input : 784 neurons → Output : 10 neurons (Probability of number being that number (0 to 9)) - In between hidden layers → activation of first layer determines activation of second layer and so on... Just how neurons in our brain work.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_1
text: **Visually:** (Neural Network: https://i.ibb.co/RGjGVsjF/nn.png) (Neural Network2: https://i.ibb.co/HDtj57cf/neural-Network-Photo.png)

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_2
text: Training data for the network will consist of many 28 * 28 pixel images of scanned handwritten digits, and so the input layer contains **784=28×28 neurons.**

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_3
text: The input pixels are greyscale, with a value of **0.0** representing **white**, a value of **1.0** representing **black**, and in between values representing gradually darkening shades of **grey.**

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_4
text: The second layer of the network is a *hidden layer*. We denote the number of neurons in this hidden layer by n, and we'll experiment with different values for n. The example shown illustrates a small hidden layer, containing just n=15 neurons.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_5
text: The output layer of the network contains 10 neurons. If the first neuron fires (i.e., has an output = digit 0) which indicates that network thinks the digit is a 0. If the second neuron fires then that will indicate that the network thinks the digit is a 1. And so on.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_6
text: You’ll notice how in these drawings each neuron from one layer is connected to each neuron of the next with a little line.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_7
text: This is meant to indicate how the activation of each neuron in one layer, the little number inside it, has some influence on the activation of each neuron in the next layer.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network_8
text: However, not all these connections are equal. Some connections are more equal than others (*shoutout George Orwell*) and determining how strong these connections are is really the heart of how a neural network operates.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_0
text: - Think about any math problem, y = x (we usually solve for x, y is known to us) - Any ML problem involves some sort of y = mx + c (slope equation of a line) where we already have y (output) and x (our sample training data), we just need to find m (slope or weights) and c (intercept or bias) so that we can fit a model to our input and get some meaningful data / insights from it.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_1
text: Question: What happens in one layer?

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_2
text: - First layer weights to next layer neuron : $w_i$ - Inputs of first layer neurons : $x_i$

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_3
text: - Calculate slope line for all, y = mx + c = $sum(w_i*x_i + bi)$ ($x_i$ is replaced by $a_i$ here after 'activating' all inputs $x_i$)

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_4
text: Weights tell you what pixel pattern this neuron in the second layer is picking up on, and the bias tells you how big that weighted sum needs to be before the neuron gets meaningfully active.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_5
text: Basic equation → y = mx + c translates to $y = sum(weights * activations + bias)$ for all neurons also this y is just a bunch of random numbers, they don't make sense, we need to squash this data into a range so that we truly can find some meaning to these. That's where activation functions come in.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_6
text: A lot of functions can do this, one of them is sigmoid which is just a fancy name for a function that translates any real-valued number to a value between 0 and 1.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_7
text: You put this $sum(weights * activations + bias) = z$ into the sigmoid activation function = $sigmoid(z)$

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_8
text: Once again: - Input : 28 * 28 = 784 neurons, Let's say I have 10 neurons in second layer. - Total : 784 (input) * 10 (neurons in second layer weights) + 10 (bias) * 10 + 10 (2nd layer) * 10 (last layer) ~ *8000* total weights and biases that can be tweaked and turned on or off per your choice.

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_9
text: Learning: Finding right weights and bias (so that our network learns underlying patterns of these numbers (i.e strokes))

id: hello world of neural networks_Neural Network Setup_10
text: The equation for a single neuron's output, often written as: $\sigma\left(\sum_i a_i w_i + b\right)$ can be cumbersome to write, especially for entire layers. We can use the tools of linear algebra—vectors and matrices—to express this much more cleanly.

id: hello world of neural networks_Representing Layers with Vectors and Matrices_2

text: * **$W^T$** is the **transpose** of the vector $W$, which turns the column vector into a row vector: $[w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n]$. * When you multiply the row vector $W^T$ by the column vector $a$, you get the exact same weighted sum:

text: Gradient descent helps neural networks learn by iteratively updating weights and biases to minimize the cost function:

id: hello world of neural networks_Revisiting the setup_16
text: $$ \mathbf{W} \leftarrow \mathbf{W} - \eta \frac{\partial C}{\partial \mathbf{W}}, \quad \mathbf{b} \leftarrow \mathbf{b} - \eta \frac{\partial C}{\partial \mathbf{b}} $$ We'll talk more about this in a while.

id: hello world of neural networks_Tuning Knobs to Minimize Loss_0
text: Imagine your model has one “knob” (parameter) $w$. Turning that knob up or down changes your model’s prediction—and thus the **loss**. Our goal is to find the setting of $w$ that makes the loss as small as possible.

id: hello world of neural networks_Tuning Knobs to Minimize Loss_1
text: Taking only one parameter : weights for now (let's say bias is fixed)

id: hello world of neural networks_Plotting Loss vs. ($w$)_0
text: - **Horizontal axis** ($x$) = parameter $w$ - **Vertical axis** ($y$) = loss $L(w)$

id: hello world of neural networks_Plotting Loss vs. ($w$)_1
text: This plot is a curve $y=L(w)$. We want the **minimum point** on that curve. (Plot: https://i.ibb.co/bgFrWDMB/Screenshot-2025-06-12-at-10-48-36-AM.png)

id: hello world of neural networks_The Derivative_0
text: The **derivative** at a point tells us the instantaneous slope of the curve:

id: hello world of neural networks_The Derivative_1
text: $$ \frac{dL}{dw} = \lim_{\Delta w \to 0} \frac{L(w + \Delta w) - L(w)}{\Delta w} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Derivative_2
text: - If $\tfrac{dL}{dw} > 0$, the curve is rising as we move right (loss increases if $w$ increases). - If $\tfrac{dL}{dw} < 0$, the curve is falling as we move right (loss decreases if $w$ increases).

id: hello world of neural networks_Ball on a Hill_0
text: Picture a ball sitting on the curve. The derivative is “which way is downhill?”

id: hello world of neural networks_Ball on a Hill_1
text: - If slope positive, the ball rolls left (decrease $w$). - If slope negative, the ball rolls right (increase $w$).

id: hello world of neural networks_Ball on a Hill_2
text: Gradient gives the direction of steepest ascend. So to minimise the function → take steps in the opposite direction.

id: hello world of neural networks_The Update Rule_0
text: We take a small step **opposite** the slope:

id: hello world of neural networks_The Update Rule_1
text: $$ w \leftarrow w - \underbrace{\eta}_{\text{learning rate}} \frac{dL}{dw} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Update Rule_2
text: - $\eta$ controls the step size.

id: hello world of neural networks_The Update Rule_3
text: - We repeat: compute slope, step downhill, repeat… until the slope is (nearly) zero.

text: - $\tfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_1}$ = rate of change if we nudge $k_1$ while keeping $k_2$ fixed. - $\tfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_2}$ = rate of change if we nudge $k_2$ while keeping $k_1$ fixed.

id: hello world of neural networks_The Gradient Vector_0
text: Collect these partials into the **gradient**:

id: hello world of neural networks_The Gradient Vector_1
text: $$ \nabla L = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_1} \\ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_2} \end{bmatrix} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Gradient Vector_2
text: - This points in the direction of **steepest ascent** on the loss surface. - To go **downhill**, we move in the **opposite** direction.

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_0
text: $$ \begin{bmatrix} k_1 \\ k_2 \end{bmatrix} \leftarrow \begin{bmatrix} k_1 \\ k_2 \end{bmatrix} - \eta\, \nabla L = \begin{bmatrix} k_1 \\ k_2 \end{bmatrix} - \eta\, \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_1} \\ \tfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_2} \end{bmatrix} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_1
text: And in **$n$-dimensional** parameter space $\mathbf{k}=(k_1,\dots,k_n)$:

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_2
text: $$ \mathbf{k} \leftarrow \mathbf{k} - \eta\, \nabla L(\mathbf{k}), \quad \nabla L(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_1} \\ \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial k_n} \end{bmatrix} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_3
text: Continuing with our *ball rolling* example: - **Draw the hill**: Visualize loss as a surface over your parameters. - **Find the slope**: Compute (partial) derivatives—these tell you “uphill” vs. “downhill.” - **Step downhill**: Update each parameter by subtracting a fraction (learning rate) of its derivative. - **Iterate**: Keep repeating until you reach a flat spot (derivative ≈ 0), i.e. a **minimum**.

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_4
text: > Gradient descent is simply “roll the ball downhill, one small step at a time.”

text: - Randomly choose starting point for a ball (imaginary) then simulate the motion of ball as it's rolled down. - We can do this by computing derivatives of cost function wrt parameters (weights and bias) : those derivatives would tell us everything about the local shape of the valley, therefore how our ball should roll. - What law or laws of motion could we pick that would make it so the ball always rolled to the bottom of the valley? where η is a small, positive parameter (known as the learning rate).

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_12
text: The learning rate $\eta$ is a parameter in neural networks that controls the size of the steps taken during gradient descent to minimize the loss function. It determines how much the weights and biases are updated in each iteration based on the computed gradients

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_13
text: Use case? Controls Step Size: The learning rate determines how large the updates to the weights and biases are. A larger learning rate results in bigger steps, while a smaller learning rate results in smaller steps.

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_14
text: A small learning rate ensures stable convergence, while a large learning rate can cause the model to overshoot the minimum.

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_15
text: Gradient Descent can be viewed as a way of taking small steps in the direction which does the most to immediately decrease Cost/Loss function. > Lets say you're at a hill and you want to go from one village to the other. And all you can see are paths. We can stand at the edge of the terrace and look for the steepest route to the terrace below. That's also the shortest path down to the next piece of level ground, if we repeat the process from terrace to terrace we will eventually reach the village. In doing so we will have taken the path of steepest descent (might not be a straight line, can be zig zag)

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_16
text: What we did was evaluate the slope/gradeint of the hillside as we looked in different directions while standing at the edge of a terrace and then took the steepest path down each time.

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_17
text: **This is gradient descent. An algorithm use to compute the minimum of the cost function.**

text: Which direction decreases C(weights, bias) most quickly?

text: Gradient/Derivative of function gives you direction of steepest increase (which dirn should you step to increase function most quickly)

text: This can be visuallied using the ball rolling diagram, draw a few slopes on the curve, - if you're on the left : you need to move right to reach the bottom - if you're on the right : you need to move left to reach the bottom (Image3: https://i.ibb.co/d4pwBVXy/Screenshot-2025-06-12-at-1-38-10-PM.png)

text: > Here is that update rule in concise mathematical form.

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_28
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)}(a^{(l-1)})^T, \quad \frac{\partial C}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_29
text: $$ \text{Compute gradients:} \quad \frac{\partial C}{\partial W}, \quad \frac{\partial C}{\partial b} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Updating again_30
text: $$ \text{Gradient‐descent update:} \quad W \leftarrow W - \eta\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial W}, \qquad b \leftarrow b - \eta\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial b} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Time 4 Math_1
text: Backpropagation is an algorithm for calculating the gradient of the cost function of a network.

id: hello world of neural networks_Time 4 Math_2
text: **Entries of gradient vector are partial derivatives of the cost function with respect to weights and biases.**

id: hello world of neural networks_Time 4 Math_3
text: Once you know how sensitive the cost function is to activations in this second-to-last layer, you can just repeat the process for all the weights and biases feeding into that layer.

id: hello world of neural networks_Time 4 Math_4
text: It’s remarkable that at the heart of every modern neural network lies nothing more exotic than a handful of basic math tools—matrix multiplication, derivatives, and the chain rule.

id: hello world of neural networks_Time 4 Math_5
text: - Matrix multiplication elegantly encodes how signals flow from one layer of neurons to the next: each weight in the matrix acts like a tiny valve, amplifying or dampening its inputs in one sweeping operation. - By defining a cost function that measures “how wrong” our network is, we turn the fuzzy notion of “learning” into the concrete problem of finding a minimum. Derivatives and gradients become our compass, pointing us downhill through a vast, multidimensional landscape of error. - And the chain rule—often dismissed in calculus class as “just another formula”—is the secret ingredient that unravels this entire web of dependencies. It lets us trace exactly how a small tweak to any weight or bias will ripple through every layer, so we can update each parameter in just the right direction.

id: hello world of neural networks_Time 4 Math_6
text: When you line up these simple ideas in the right order, you get back-propagation—and with it, the ability to build systems that can recognize images, translate languages, and more.

id: hello world of neural networks_Sensitivity of the Cost to a Single Weight_0
text: Our **goal** is to measure how a tiny change (“nudge”) in one weight in the last layer, $w^{(L)}$, affects the loss $C$. In calculus terms we want the partial derivative:

metadata.section: Sensitivity of the Cost to a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_Sensitivity of the Cost to a Single Weight_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(L)}} $$

metadata.section: Sensitivity of the Cost to a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_Sensitivity of the Cost to a Single Weight_2
text: When you see $\partial w^{(L)}$, think “a small nudge to $w^{(L)}$”; when you see $\partial C$, think “the resulting nudge to the cost.” Their ratio $\tfrac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(L)}}$ is the **instantaneous rate of change** of the loss with respect to that weight.

metadata.section: Sensitivity of the Cost to a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Chain Rule Decomposition_0
text: Because $C$ depends on $w^{(L)}$ only through the pre‐activation $z^{(L)}$ and the activation $a^{(L)}$, the chain rule gives

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Chain Rule Decomposition_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(L)}} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial a^{(L)}} \;\times\; \frac{\partial a^{(L)}}{\partial z^{(L)}} \;\times\; \frac{\partial z^{(L)}}{\partial w^{(L)}}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Chain Rule Decomposition_2
text: A neat trick to verify if this is right is to cancel all denom and next numerator from the start, you'll get the original function.

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Individual Derivatives_0
text: 1. **Pre‐activation**

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Individual Derivatives_1
text: $$ z^{(L)} = w^{(L)}a^{(L-1)} + b^{(L)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial z^{(L)}}{\partial w^{(L)}} = a^{(L-1)}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Individual Derivatives_2
text: 2. **Activation (sigmoid)**

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Individual Derivatives_3
text: $$ a^{(L)} = \sigma\left(z^{(L)}\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial a^{(L)}}{\partial z^{(L)}} = \sigma'\left(z^{(L)}\right) = \sigma\left(z^{(L)}\right)\left(1 - \sigma\left(z^{(L)}\right)\right). $$

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Individual Derivatives_4
text: 3. **Loss for one example** (Mean Squared Error)

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Individual Derivatives_5
text: $$ C_0 = \left(a^{(L)} - y\right)^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial C_0}{\partial a^{(L)}} = 2\left(a^{(L)} - y\right). $$

id: hello world of neural networks_3. Combined Gradient_0
text: Putting it all together,

id: hello world of neural networks_3. Combined Gradient_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial C_0}{\partial w^{(L)}} = \underbrace{2\bigl(a^{(L)} - y\bigr)}_{\frac{\partial C_0}{\partial a^{(L)}}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\sigma'\!\bigl(z^{(L)}\bigr)}_{\frac{\partial a^{(L)}}{\partial z^{(L)}}} \;\times\; \underbrace{a^{(L-1)}}_{\frac{\partial z^{(L)}}{\partial w^{(L)}}} \;=\; 2\,\bigl(a^{(L)} - y\bigr)\,\sigma'\!\bigl(z^{(L)}\bigr)\,a^{(L-1)}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_3. Combined Gradient_2
text: This tells us **exactly** how a small change in $w^{(L)}$ for one training example will change the loss.

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Averaging Over the Dataset_0
text: For $N$ training examples, we average these per–example gradients to get the gradient of the full cost $C$:

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Averaging Over the Dataset_1
text: $$ \nabla C = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial C^{(i)}}{\partial w^{(L)}}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_5. Update Rule (Gradient Descent)_0
text: Finally, we update the weight by stepping **opposite** to the gradient:

id: hello world of neural networks_5. Update Rule (Gradient Descent)_1
text: $$ w^{(L)} \;\leftarrow\; w^{(L)} \;-\;\eta\, \frac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(L)}}, $$ where $\eta$ is the learning rate. Likewise for the bias: $$ b^{(L)} \;\leftarrow\; b^{(L)} \;-\;\eta\, \frac{\partial C}{\partial b^{(L)}}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Stochastic Gradient Descent:_0
text: When your dataset is huge, computing the exact gradient $\displaystyle \nabla C = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla C^{(i)}$ on all $N$ examples each update can be very slow. **Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)** speeds things up by estimating the true gradient with a small random **mini-batch** of $m\ll N$ examples:

id: hello world of neural networks_Stochastic Gradient Descent:_1
text: $$ \nabla C_{\text{batch}} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\in\text{batch}}\nabla C^{(i)}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Stochastic Gradient Descent:_2
text: 1.**Sample** a mini-batch of $m$ training examples at random. 2.**Compute** the average gradient $\nabla C_{\text{batch}}$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Stochastic Gradient Descent:_3
text: $$ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla C_{\text{batch}} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Stochastic Gradient Descent:_4
text: where $\eta$ is the learning rate.

id: hello world of neural networks_Why It Works_0
text: - **Cost per update** falls from $O(N)$ to $O(m)$. - **Unbiased estimate**: $\mathbb{E}[\nabla C_{\text{batch}}] = \nabla C$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Why It Works_1
text: > Stochastic GD is like political polling: > it’s far cheaper to poll 1,000 voters (a mini-batch) > than to canvass an entire electorate (the full dataset), > yet the poll’s average still points in the right direction.

id: hello world of neural networks_Partial Derivative w.r.t. Bias_0
text: For a neuron with pre-activation $$ z = W\,x \;+\; b, $$ the bias $b$ enters **linearly**, so

id: hello world of neural networks_Partial Derivative w.r.t. Bias_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial z}{\partial b} \;=\; 1 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \frac{\partial C}{\partial b} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial b} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_0
text: We’ve already seen how to compute two entries of the gradient vector for the **last** layer: 1. **Weight gradient**

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial W^{(L)}} = \delta^{(L)}\,(a^{(L-1)})^{\top} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_2
text: 2. **Bias gradient**

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_3
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial b^{(L)}} = \delta^{(L)} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_4
text: where $\delta^{(L)} = \tfrac{\partial C}{\partial z^{(L)}}$.

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_5
text: By **propagating** these errors backward through the network—multiplying along the chain of dependencies—we obtain every partial derivative $\tfrac{\partial C}{\partial w}$ and $\tfrac{\partial C}{\partial b}$ for **every** layer. Stacking them gives the **gradient vector**:

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_6
text: $$ \nabla C \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} \vdots \\ \displaystyle \frac{\partial C}{\partial w_1} \\ \displaystyle \frac{\partial C}{\partial b_1} \\ \vdots \end{bmatrix}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_7
text: Once we have $\nabla C$, we perform **gradient descent** (or SGD) to step **downhill** and minimize the loss:

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_8
text: $$ \theta \;\leftarrow\; \theta \;-\;\eta\,\nabla C. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_9
text: *Components of gradient vector guide the adjustments we need to make.*

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_10
text: If for a particular configuration: - The partial derivative of loss with respect to k1 is positive means increase k1 implies increase in loss - Hence we need to decrease (opposite sign of gradient) k1 to decrease loss.

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_11
text: How do we access the derivative of the loss function in the first place? **Chain Rule** → tells you how to compute derivative of combination of functions.

id: hello world of neural networks_The Full Gradient Vector_12
text: The **chain rule** tells us how to compute the derivative of a function that is itself the input to another function. In symbols, if $$ h(x) = f\bigl(g(x)\bigr), $$ then $$ \frac{d}{dx}h(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\bigl[f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\bigr] = f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\;\cdot\;g'(x). $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Intuition: Two “Machines” in Series_0
text: 1. **Machine 1**

id: hello world of neural networks_Intuition: Two “Machines” in Series_1
text: - Input: $x$ - Output: $g(x)$ - Local slope: $g'(x)$

id: hello world of neural networks_Intuition: Two “Machines” in Series_2
text: 2. **Machine 2**

id: hello world of neural networks_Intuition: Two “Machines” in Series_3
text: - Input: $u = g(x)$ - Output: $f(u)$ - Local slope: $f'(u)$

id: hello world of neural networks_Intuition: Two “Machines” in Series_4
text: When you feed $x$ into the first machine, it spits out $g(x)$. That becomes the input to the second machine, which outputs $f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_0
text: 1. **Nudge** $x$ by a tiny amount $\Delta x$. 2. **Machine 1** outputs

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_1
text: $$ g(x + \Delta x) \approx g(x) + g'(x)\,\Delta x $$ So the **change** in its output is $$ \Delta u \approx g'(x)\,\Delta x, $$ where $u = g(x)$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_2
text: 3. **Machine 2** then sees its input change by $\Delta u$, so its output changes by

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_3
text: $$ f(u + \Delta u) \approx f(u) + f'(u)\,\Delta u $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_4
text: 4. **Combined change** in the final output:

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_5
text: $$ \Delta h = f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,\Delta u \approx f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,\bigl[g'(x)\,\Delta x\bigr] = \bigl[f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,g'(x)\bigr]\,\Delta x $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_6
text: 5. Dividing by $\Delta x$ and taking the limit $\Delta x \to 0$ gives the chain rule:

id: hello world of neural networks_Small Nudge Argument_7
text: $$ \frac{d}{dx}f\bigl(g(x)\bigr) = f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr) \cdot g'(x) $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Why is it fast?_0
text: In what sense is backpropagation a fast algorithm? To answer this question, let's consider another approach to computing the gradient.

id: hello world of neural networks_Why is it fast?_1
text: Imagine it's the early days of neural networks research. Maybe it's the 1950s or 1960s, and you're the first person in the world to think of using gradient descent to learn! But to make the idea work you need a way of computing the gradient of the cost function.

id: hello world of neural networks_Why is it fast?_2
text: You think back to your knowledge of calculus, and decide to see if you can use the chain rule to compute the gradient. But after playing around a bit, the algebra looks complicated, and you get discouraged.

id: hello world of neural networks_Why is it fast?_3
text: So you try to find another approach. You decide to regard the cost as a function of the weights C=C(w) alone (we'll get back to the biases in a moment). You number the weights w1,w2,…, and want to compute ∂C/∂wj for some particular weight wj. An obvious way of doing that is to use the approximation where ϵ>0 is a small positive number, and ej is the unit vector in the jth direction. In other words, we can estimate ∂C/∂wj by computing the cost C for two slightly different values of wj.

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Bruteforce Gradient Descent_0
text: To estimate $\tfrac{\partial C}{\partial w_j}$ by finite differences, you’d do

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Bruteforce Gradient Descent_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial w_j} \approx \frac{C\bigl(w + \varepsilon\,e_j\bigr)\;-\;C(w)}{\varepsilon}, $$

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Bruteforce Gradient Descent_2
text: where $e_j$ is the unit vector in direction $j$. If you have \(N\) weights, that requires $N+1$ full forward‐passes through the network per training example!

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Backpropagation via the Chain Rule_0
text: Backprop avoids that explosion by **computing all** partial derivatives $\tfrac{\partial C}{\partial w_j}$ at once with:

id: hello world of neural networks_2. Backpropagation via the Chain Rule_1
text: 1. **One forward pass** (compute all activations). 2. **One backward pass** (propagate “error signals” and multiply local derivatives).

id: hello world of neural networks_2.1 Small‐Change Analysis_0
text: A small change $\Delta w_{l,j,k}$ in weight $w_{l,j,k}$ causes a small change in the neuron’s activation:

id: hello world of neural networks_2.1 Small‐Change Analysis_1
text: $$ \Delta a_{l,j} \approx \frac{\partial a_{l,j}}{\partial w_{l,j,k}}\, \Delta w_{l,j,k}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_2.1 Small‐Change Analysis_2
text: That, in turn, perturbs the next layer’s activation:

id: hello world of neural networks_2.1 Small‐Change Analysis_3
text: $$ \Delta a_{l+1,q} \approx \frac{\partial a_{l+1,q}}{\partial a_{l,j}}\, \Delta a_{l,j}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_2.1 Small‐Change Analysis_4
text: … and so on, all the way to the cost \(C\):

id: hello world of neural networks_2.1 Small‐Change Analysis_5
text: $$ \Delta C \approx \frac{\partial C}{\partial w_{l,j,k}}\, \Delta w_{l,j,k}. $$

id: hello world of neural networks_2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight_0
text: By following **every path** from $w_{l,j,k}$ to the final cost, and **multiplying** the local partials along each edge, then **summing** over all such paths, you get:

metadata.section: 2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight_1
text: $$ \frac{\partial C}{\partial w_{l,j,k}} = \sum_{\text{paths }p} \prod_{\substack{\text{edges }(u\to v)\\\in p}} \frac{\partial v}{\partial u}. $$

metadata.section: 2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight_2
text: Backpropagation is simply a dynamic‐programming implementation of this sum‐of‐products **in linear time** $O(N)$, rather than $O(N^2)$ or worse.

metadata.section: 2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight_3
text: - **Finite‐difference**: $O(N)$ forward passes for $N$ weights → **slow**. - **Backpropagation**: 1 forward pass + 1 backward pass → **fast**. - Uses the **chain rule** to share and reuse intermediate derivatives, computing the entire gradient vector $\nabla C$ efficiently.

metadata.section: 2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight_4
text: *Backpropagation algorithm as providing a way of computing the sum over the rate factor for all these paths. Or, to put it slightly differently, the backpropagation algorithm is a clever way of keeping track of small perturbations to the weights (and biases) as they propagate through the network, reach the output, and then affect the cost.*

metadata.section: 2.2 Chain Rule for a Single Weight

id: hello world of neural networks_Vanishing Gradient Problem_0
text: So what happens when you backprop? You are essentially using an activation function (sigmoid/tanh) to squash numbers between 0 to 1 and then using chain rule multiply them to achieve backpropagation.

id: hello world of neural networks_Vanishing Gradient Problem_1
text: If you have multiple (ALOT) of layers & you're doing this → The value at which the initail weights learn (by the time it gets there) becomes close to 0 so they don't end up learning.

id: hello world of neural networks_Vanishing Gradient Problem_2
text: If you're using sigmoid activations in a deep network, and many of your neurons' inputs fall into the "saturated" regions, their derivatives will be close to zero (e.g., 0.1, 0.01, or even smaller).

id: hello world of neural networks_Vanishing Gradient Problem_3
text: When you multiply many such small numbers together during backpropagation (e.g., $0.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.25 \dots$), the result becomes an extremely small number very quickly.

id: hello world of neural networks_Vanishing Gradient Problem_4
text: This "vanishing" gradient means that the weights in the early layers receive an almost zero gradient signal and the network never really learns anything.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_0
text: Negative Input: If the weighted sum of inputs to a ReLU neuron (before applying the activation function) is negative, the ReLU function will output 0 (defination of $RelU : f(a) = max(0, a)$)

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_1
text: *Zero Gradient:* When the output is 0, the derivative of the ReLU function with respect to its input is also 0.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_2
text: During backpropagation, the gradient of the loss with respect to the neuron's weights and biases is calculated by multiplying the upstream gradient with the local gradient.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_3
text: If the local gradient is 0, then the gradients for the weights and biases connected to this neuron become 0.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_4
text: *No Weight Updates:* If the gradients are 0, the weights and biases of that neuron will not be updated during subsequent training iterations.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_5
text: Permanent Inactivity: This means the neuron is effectively "dead." It will always output 0, regardless of the input, and it will never learn or contribute to the network's learning process. It's stuck in an inactive state.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_6
text: Solution to this? Use Leaky ReLU function which never gets 0.

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_7
text: $$ f(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x > 0 \\ \alpha x & \text{if } x \leq 0 \end{cases} $$ Where:

id: hello world of neural networks_Dead Neuron Problem_8
text: - $x$: Input to the activation function. - $\alpha$: A small positive constant (e.g., $(0.01$) that determines the slope for negative input values.

id: hello world of neural networks_Optional_3
text: If you've read this entirely, this is going to make a lot of sense.

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_0
text: Let's define the operations for a single neuron:

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_1
text: - **Linear Combination:** $z = Wx + b$, where $W$ is the weight, $x$ is the input, and $b$ is the bias. - **Activation:** $a = \sigma(z)$, where $a$ is the activation (this is basically the `predicted_output`). The activation function $\sigma$ can be sigmoid, ReLU, etc.—anything that squashes our function into the range $[0, 1]$. - **Loss:** $L = \text{loss}(a, y)$, where $L$ is a function of two things: the predicted output $a$ and the actual output $y$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_2
text: **Chain Rule: Calculating the Gradient of the Loss**

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_3
text: How does the loss $L$ change with respect to the weight $W$ and bias $b$? The loss depends on $W$ only through the activation $a$ and the linear combination $z$. We can trace this dependency: $L \leftarrow a \leftarrow z \leftarrow W$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_4
text: The chain rule gives us: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial W} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_5
text: Let's calculate these three values individually:

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_6
text: 1. **$\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}$** This measures how the loss changes if you wiggle the neuron's output. For a simple squared error loss $L = \frac{1}{2}(a - y)^2$, this derivative is:

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_7
text: Isn't Loss supposed to be (a - y)^2 ? Why is the $1/2$ there?

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_8
text: The $\frac{1}{2}$ is included for mathematical convenience during differentiation.

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_9
text: When you take the derivative of $L = \frac{1}{2}(a - y)^2$ with respect to \(a\), using the chain rule:

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_10
text: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} = \frac{\partial}{\partial a} \left( \frac{1}{2}(a - y)^2 \right) $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_11
text: Bring the exponent down: $$ \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot (a - y)^{2-1} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_12
text: Multiply by the derivative of the inside $a-y$ with respect to $a$, which is $1$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_13
text: So, the derivative becomes: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot (a - y) \cdot 1 $$ Which simplifies to: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} = (a - y) $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_14
text: The 1/2 neatly cancels out the $2$ that comes from differentiating the square term.

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_15
text: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} = a - y $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_16
text: 2. **$\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}$** This is the derivative of the activation function. For a sigmoid function:

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_17
text: $$ \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} = \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z)) $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_18
text: 3. **$\frac{\partial z}{\partial W}$** Since $z = Wx + b$, the partial derivative with respect to $W$ is just $x$:

id: hello world of neural networks_Single Neuron Chain Rule_19
text: $$ \frac{\partial z}{\partial W} = x $$

id: hello world of neural networks_For Multiple Layers_0
text: Now let's consider a simple network: input $x$ $\rightarrow$ hidden layer $h$ $\rightarrow$ output $\hat{y}$

id: hello world of neural networks_For Multiple Layers_1
text: - **Hidden Layer:** $h = \sigma(z^{(1)}) = \sigma(W^{(1)}x + b^{(1)})$ - **Output Layer:** $\hat{y} = \sigma(z^{(2)}) = \sigma(W^{(2)}h + b^{(2)})$ - **Loss:** $L = \text{loss}(\hat{y}, y)$

id: hello world of neural networks_For Multiple Layers_2
text: To find the gradient with respect to the first layer's weights, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}}$, we need a longer chain rule: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}} = \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial h} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial z^{(1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{(1)}}{\partial W^{(1)}} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Backpropagation: The Full Process_0
text: 1. **Forward Pass:** Compute all \(z\) values (linear equations) and \(a\) values (activations) for all layers, from input to output. 2. **Initialise:** Set $\frac{\partial L}{\partial L} = 1$. This seeds the chain rule so that every other partial derivative in the graph gets scaled correctly. You want to find $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}$, which can be thought of as $\frac{\partial L}{\partial L} \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial W}$.

id: hello world of neural networks_Backpropagation: The Full Process_1
text: 3. **Backward Pass:** For each node in reverse topological order (from output to input), call its local derivative function to propagate the "error" or "gradient" to its inputs, and use this to calculate the gradients for the node's parameters (weights and bias).

id: hello world of neural networks_Backpropagation: The Full Process_2
text: - one input layer $x$ (column vector) - one hidden layer (weights $W^{(1)},\; b^{(1)}$) - one output layer (weights $W^{(2)},\; b^{(2)}$) - a sigmoid activation $\sigma(\cdot)$ everywhere - a mean-squared-error loss

id: hello world of neural networks_Backpropagation: The Full Process_3
text: You can extend exactly the same logic to deeper nets.

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Forward pass_0
text: The network prediction $\hat{y}$ is produced in three little steps.

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Forward pass_1
text: 1. Hidden-layer pre-activation $z^{(1)} = W^{(1)}x + b^{(1)}$

id: hello world of neural networks_1. Forward pass_2
text: 2. Hidden activation $h = \sigma\!\bigl(z^{(1)}\bigr)$

id: hello world of neural networks_3. Back-propagation: the 4 core equations_0
text: Back-prop simply applies the chain rule from right to left, layer by layer.

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ① Output-layer error_0
text: $$ \delta^{(2)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}} = (\hat{y} - y)\,\sigma'\bigl(z^{(2)}\bigr) $$

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ① Output-layer error_1
text: *“How much does the loss change if I nudge the output neuron’s input up or down?”*

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ② Gradients for output weights and bias_0
text: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)}\,h^{\top}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)} $$

metadata.section: Eq ② Gradients for output weights and bias

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ② Gradients for output weights and bias_1
text: *“Each weight in layer 2 matters in proportion to the hidden activation it multiplies.”*

metadata.section: Eq ② Gradients for output weights and bias

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ③ Propagate the error back to the hidden layer_0
text: $$ \delta^{(1)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(1)}} = \left(W^{(2)}\right)^{\top} \delta^{(2)} \odot \sigma'\bigl(z^{(1)}\bigr) $$

metadata.section: Eq ③ Propagate the error back to the hidden layer

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ③ Propagate the error back to the hidden layer_1
text: ($\odot$ = element-wise product : basically matrix multiplication done wrong) *“Hidden neurons are blamed for the final error in proportion to how strongly they feed it and how steep their own sigmoid is.”*

metadata.section: Eq ③ Propagate the error back to the hidden layer

id: hello world of neural networks_Eq ④ Gradients for first-layer weights and bias_0
text: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)}\,x^{\top}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)} $$

metadata.section: Eq ④ Gradients for first-layer weights and bias

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Parameter update  (Gradient Descent step)_0
text: With learning rate $\eta$:

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Parameter update  (Gradient Descent step)_1
text: $$ W^{(i)} \leftarrow W^{(i)} - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(i)}}, \qquad b^{(i)} \leftarrow b^{(i)} - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(i)}}, \quad i \in \{1, 2\} $$

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Parameter update  (Gradient Descent step)_2
text: This finishes one training iteration: forward → compute loss → apply the four back-prop equations → update.

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Parameter update  (Gradient Descent step)_3
text: Back-prop is nothing more than “apply the chain rule repeatedly”.

id: hello world of neural networks_4. Parameter update  (Gradient Descent step)_4
text: - Eq ① makes the final layer aware of its mistake. - Eq ② turns that mistake into gradients for its own parameters. - Eq ③ pushes the blame backwards. - Eq ④ turns that earlier blame into earlier gradients, and finally we step the parameters downhill with gradient descent.

id: understanding object detection_intro_0
text: Say you're on the street, in just milliseconds you spot a car, man, traffic light, dogs etc.. you don't just see a mash of pixels, you see *objects*. You know where they are, what they are and how they're moving. How can you teach a computer the same thing?

id: understanding object detection_intro_1
text: For a long time, teaching a computer to do this was a painfully slow process. Early models were like a detective with a magnifying glass, scanning an image patch by patch, asking, "Is this a car? No. Is *this* a car? No." It worked, but it was slow.

id: understanding object detection_intro_2
text: In 2016, a paper came out with a name: **You Only Look Once (YOLO)**.

id: understanding object detection_intro_3
text: The name says it all. What if, instead of looking at an image thousands of times, a computer could just... look once? This post is the story of that idea. This blog discusses YOLO, figures out *why* it works, and see where it stumbles. This also consists of the history of YOLO models and how we have reached state-of-the-art YOLOv10 model of today.

id: understanding object detection_Traditional Computer Vision_0
text: Earlier approaches picked up patterns based on mathematical features from images in matrix form. We figured out where hue, contrast, and pixel density were high and used that to classify images (using models like ResNet).

id: understanding object detection_Traditional Computer Vision_1
text: **The Problem:** This doesn't work well for complex scenarios like CCTV footage with:

id: understanding object detection_Traditional Computer Vision_2
text: - Dozens of objects - Heavy occlusion - Complex features - Real-time requirements (ResNet takes huge amounts of time even during inference)

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_0
text: Then came the two-stage detection pipeline:

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_1
text: The convolutional feature map contains high-level semantic information about the image. The first stage generates potential object locations (proposals), and the second stage refines these proposals and assigns class labels.

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_2
text: **Why "Two-Stage"?** The first pass generates a set of proposals (potential object locations), and the second pass refines these proposals to make final predictions.

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_3
text: **Advantages:**

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_4
text: - More accurate than previous methods - Each component can be optimized separately

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_5
text: **Disadvantages:**

id: understanding object detection_Two-Stage Detectors: R-CNN & Faster R-CNN_6
text: - Multi-stage pipeline is complex - Each component trained separately - Not suitable for real-time applications (~5 fps on GPU) - Computationally expensive

id: understanding object detection_Why YOLO: The Motivation_0
text: Core Idea: **What if we could do object detection as a single regression problem?**

id: understanding object detection_Why YOLO: The Motivation_1
text: Instead of:

id: understanding object detection_Why YOLO: The Motivation_2
text: 1. Generate proposals → 2. Classify proposals

id: understanding object detection_Why YOLO: The Motivation_3
text: Do: **Single network → Box detection + Category prediction simultaneously**

id: understanding object detection_Key Advantages of Single-Stage Detection:_0
text: - **Speed**: One forward pass through the network - **Simplicity**: End-to-end training with a unified loss function - **Global reasoning**: The network sees the entire image, understanding context - **Real-time performance**: 45+ fps (compared to 5 fps for two-stage detectors)

id: understanding object detection_The Trade-off:_0
text: - Slightly lower accuracy on metrics

id: understanding object detection_The Trade-off:_1
text: YOLO was created by Ultralytics (2016) to solve this problem: a single network that can perform both box detection and category prediction in one pass.

id: understanding object detection_YOLO High Level Overview_0
text: YOLO (You Only Look Once) reformulates object detection as a **single regression problem**:

id: understanding object detection_Concept_0
text: 1. **Input**: Image of any size (resized to 448×448) 2. **Process**: Divide image into S×S grid cells (S=7 in the paper) 3. **Predict**: For each grid cell, predict B bounding boxes and C class probabilities 4. **Output**: Tensor of shape S×S×(B×5+C)

id: understanding object detection_Why "You Only Look Once"?_0
text: Unlike sliding window approaches (like DPM) that run a classifier at every position, or two-stage detectors that process thousands of region proposals, YOLO looks at the image **once** in a single forward pass.

id: understanding object detection_Single Pass, End-to-End_0
text: - No separate proposal generation - No batch processing of regions - One network, one forward pass - Direct prediction from pixels to bounding boxes and classes (YOLO High-Level Pipeline: /assets/images/yolo/basic.png)

id: understanding object detection_Single Pass, End-to-End_1
text: *Figure: YOLO's single-stage detection pipeline - the entire image is processed once to produce bounding boxes and class predictions* (YOLO Algorithm Overview: /assets/images/yolo/yoloAlgo.png)

id: understanding object detection_Single Pass, End-to-End_2
text: *Figure: The complete YOLO detection algorithm from input image to final predictions*

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_0
text: At its heart, YOLO is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_1
text: CNN Analogy:: Think of it like a company's hierarchy, designed to process information from the ground up.

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_2
text: 1. **The Interns (Early Layers):** The first few layers of the network are like interns. They get the raw image and have a very simple job: find basic patterns. One intern looks for vertical edges, another for horizontal edges, another for patches of green, and so on. They're not smart, but they're fast and there are a lot of them.

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_3
text: 2. **The Mid-Level Managers (Deeper Layers):** These layers take the simple reports from the interns and combine them into more complex ideas. A manager might see reports for a sharp corner, a curved line, and a circular shape and say, "Hmm, that's starting to look like an eye." Another might combine reports of four straight lines and a rectangle to identify a "window."

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_4
text: 3. **The CEO (Final Layers):** The final layers are the executives. They take the high-level reports from the managers ("we've got an eye," "we've got a furry texture," "we've got a wet nose") and make the final call: "That's a dog."

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_5
text: YOLO's architecture is essentially a 24-layer version of this, followed by 2 "fully connected" layers which act like the final board meeting where all the information is synthesized into the final output.

id: understanding object detection_The "Brain" of YOLO: The Architecture_7

text: **Detection Head:**

text: - **2 fully connected layers** (4096 neurons → 1470 neurons) - **Linear activation** on the final layer (CNN Visualization: /assets/images/yolo/cnn.png)

id: understanding object detection_Why Stack Convolutional Layers?_0
text: **Purpose**: Extract spatial features from the image while preserving structure.

id: understanding object detection_Why Stack Convolutional Layers?_1
text: **The Problem**: Simply stacking convolutions doesn't increase non-linearity in the data.

id: understanding object detection_Why Stack Convolutional Layers?_2
text: **The Solution**:

id: understanding object detection_Why Stack Convolutional Layers?_3
text: - Use **non-linear activation functions** (Leaky ReLU) between layers - Use **1×1 convolutions** to reduce dimensionality and add non-linearity - Use **3×3 convolutions** to extract spatial features and downsample

id: understanding object detection_Why Leaky ReLU?_0
text: Standard ReLU: `f(x) = max(0, x)` → can cause "dying neurons" (always output 0)

id: understanding object detection_Why Leaky ReLU?_1
text: Leaky ReLU: `f(x) = x if x > 0 else 0.1*x` → allows small negative gradients, preventing dead neurons

id: understanding object detection_How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship_0
text: So how does it "look once"? The core idea is surprisingly simple and elegant. It's like a high-stakes, super-fast game of Battleship.

metadata.section: How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship

id: understanding object detection_How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship_1
text: Here's the game plan:

metadata.section: How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship

id: understanding object detection_How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship_2
text: 1.**Take the image and lay a grid over it.** The original YOLO uses a 7x7 grid. This divides the image into 49 cells.

metadata.section: How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship

id: understanding object detection_How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship_3
text: 2.**Each grid cell gets a job.** It's responsible for detecting any object whose *center point* falls within that cell. It's like each square on the Battleship board is responsible for reporting if the center of a ship is in it.

metadata.section: How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship

id: understanding object detection_How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship_4
text: 3.**Make a prediction for every cell.** A single, powerful neural network looks at the whole image and, for every single one of the 49 grid cells, it spits out a prediction. This prediction answers a few key questions: - "Is an object's center in here? How confident am I?" - "If so, where is the bounding box for that object?" - "And what class is it (a dog, a person, a car)?"

metadata.section: How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship

id: understanding object detection_How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship_5
text: That's it. One look, one pass through the network, and out comes a flood of predictions from all 49 cells at once. No proposals, no second stage. Just a direct mapping from image pixels to bounding boxes and class probabilities.

metadata.section: How YOLO Works: A Game of Battleship

id: understanding object detection_Example_3

id: understanding object detection_Example_4
text: This is a fundamental rule of the original YOLO. Even though each cell will propose two bounding boxes (we'll get to that), it can only have one final opinion on the class of the object. It's like a square on the Battleship board that can only shout "Hit!" for one ship, even if two ships happen to cross over it.

id: understanding object detection_Example_5

id: understanding object detection_Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)_0
text: **The Problem**: Multiple grid cells often detect the same object, creating duplicate/redundant boxes.

id: understanding object detection_Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)_1
text: **The Solution**: Keep only the box with the highest confidence and remove all others that significantly overlap with it. (NMS Process: /assets/images/yolo/nms.png)

id: understanding object detection_NMS Algorithm_0
text: For each class separately:

id: understanding object detection_NMS Algorithm_1
text: 1. **Sort** all detections by confidence (descending) 2. **Select** the box with highest confidence 3. **Remove** all boxes with `IOU > threshold` (e.g., 0.5) with the selected box 4. **Repeat** until no boxes remain

id: understanding object detection_NMS Algorithm_2
text: **Why per-class?** We want to suppress duplicate detections of the same object, but not suppress a person detection because it overlaps with a car detection.

id: understanding object detection_NMS Algorithm_3
text: > **Picking NMS Threshold** > > Choosing the wrong IOU threshold for NMS drastically affects performance. > > **Threshold too low** (e.g., 0.3):

id: understanding object detection_NMS Algorithm_5
text: > - Suppresses too few boxes > - **Result**: Multiple boxes per object (duplicates) > - **Example**: Single person gets 3 bounding boxes > > **Paper uses 0.5**:

id: understanding object detection_NMS Algorithm_6
text: > - Balances duplicate suppression and multi-object detection > - Works well for most scenarios > > **NMS Intuition**: Imagine a talent show where multiple judges rate the same performance. NMS is like keeping only the judge with the highest score and ignoring others who rated the same performance. This prevents counting the same act multiple times.

id: understanding object detection_Why Regression Loss?_0
text: Object detection in YOLO is formulated as a **regression problem**: we're predicting continuous values (box coordinates, confidence scores, class probabilities).

id: understanding object detection_Why Regression Loss?_1
text: The loss function uses **Mean Squared Error (MSE)** for all components, but with careful weighting to handle class imbalance and scale differences.

id: understanding object detection_Three Components of Loss_0
text: 1. **Localization Loss**: Ensures predicted box coordinates match ground truth 2. **Confidence Loss**: Trains confidence scores to reflect object presence and fit quality 3. **Classification Loss**: Ensures correct class probabilities for cells with objects

id: understanding object detection_Three Components of Loss_1
text: **Total Loss** = λ_coord × L_box + L_conf + L_class

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_0
text: **Problem**: In most images, most grid cells don't contain objects.

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_1
text: - ~2-5 cells with objects - ~44-47 cells without objects

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_2
text: **Impact**:

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_3
text: - Gradients from "no object" cells dominate training - Overwhelms gradients from "object" cells - Network learns to predict "no object" everywhere

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_4
text: **Solution**: Weight the losses differently

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_5
text: - **λ_coord = 5**: Increase weight of box coordinate loss - **λ_noobj = 0.5**: Decrease weight of "no object" confidence loss

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_6
text: > **Intuition: Why λ_coord = 5 and λ_noobj = 0.5?** > > **The Numbers Game**:

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_7
text: > - Typical image: 2-3 cells with objects, 46-47 cells without objects > - Ratio: ~20:1 (no-object : object) > > **Without weighting** (all λ = 1):

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_8
text: > ```text > Total confidence loss = 2 × (object conf loss) + 47 × (no-object conf loss) > ≈ 2 × 0.5 + 47 × 0.1 = 5.7 > ≈ 82% from no-object cells! > ```

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_9
text: > The "no object" gradient overwhelms "object" gradient → network learns to predict "no object" everywhere. > > **With weighting** (λ_coord=5, λ_noobj=0.5):

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_10
text: > ```text > Box coord loss: 5 × (2 cells × coord error) = 5 × 1.0 = 5.0 > Object conf loss: 1 × (2 cells × conf error) = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 > No-obj conf loss: 0.5 × (47 cells × conf error) = 0.5 × 4.7 = 2.35 > Total ≈ 7.85, where localization now matters most. > ``` > > **Why these specific values?**

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_11
text: > - **λ_coord = 5**: Emphasizes getting boxes right (5× more important than classification) > - **λ_noobj = 0.5**: De-emphasizes empty cells (2× less important than object cells) > - Balance found empirically through ablation studies in the paper > > **Intuition**: Like a teacher grading homework — give more points for correct answers (λ_coord=5), fewer points for saying "I don't know" (λ_noobj=0.5).

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_12
text: > **Wrong Lambda Values** > > **Mistake #1**: Using λ_coord = 1 (same as others)

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_13
text: > - **Result**: Network struggles with localization. Boxes are detected but poorly positioned. > - **Symptom**: Low IOU scores even when objects are detected > > **Mistake #2**: Using λ_noobj = 1 (same as object cells)

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_14
text: > - **Result**: No-object gradient dominates, network predicts low confidence for everything > - **Symptom**: Very few detections, even on objects that are clearly visible > > **Mistake #3**: Using λ_coord = 10 (too high)

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_15
text: > - **Result**: Network focuses only on boxes, ignores classification > - **Symptom**: Good IOU but wrong class labels > > **How to tune**: Start with paper values (5, 0.5). Only adjust if you have domain-specific reasons (e.g., small dataset → increase λ_coord to 7). (Loss Penalty Weighting: /assets/images/yolo/loss_penalty.png)

id: understanding object detection_The Class Imbalance Problem_16
text: *Figure: Visualization of class imbalance problem - most grid cells (gray) contain no objects while only a few (colored) contain objects, showing why we need λ weighting factors*

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_0
text: **Goal**: Make predicted box coordinates close to ground truth.

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_1
text: **Formula**:

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_2
text: Where:

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_3
text: - `𝟙ᵢⱼᵒᵇʲ` = 1 if cell i contains an object and box j is responsible for it - `(x, y, w, h)` = ground truth box coordinates (YOLO format) - `(x̂, ŷ, ŵ, ĥ)` = predicted box coordinates - **Responsible box** = the box with highest IOU with ground truth

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_4
text: **Why square root of w and h?**

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_5
text: **Problem**: MSE treats errors equally regardless of box size.

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_6
text: - 10-pixel error in 100×100 box = small mistake - 10-pixel error in 20×20 box = huge mistake

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_7
text: **Solution**: Predict √w and √h instead of w and h directly.

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_8
text: - Small boxes: √w changes more for same absolute change - Large boxes: √w changes less for same absolute change - This makes errors more balanced across different box sizes

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_9
text: **Example**:

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_10
text: - Box 1: w=100, √w=10, error of 10 → √110 - 10 = 0.49 - Box 2: w=25, √w=5, error of 10 → √35 - 5 = 0.92 (penalized more)

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_11
text: > **Intuition: Why √w and √h?** > > **The Problem**: Absolute errors matter more for small objects. > > Imagine two prediction errors:

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_12
text: > - **Large box** (200×200 pixels): Predicted width = 210, GT = 200 → error = 10 pixels > - **Small box** (20×20 pixels): Predicted width = 30, GT = 20 → error = 10 pixels > > Both have the same **absolute error** (10 pixels), but the small box error is **much worse** (50% error vs 5% error)! > > **Without √**: MSE treats both equally → Loss = 10² = 100 for both. > > **With √**: Square root scaling makes errors proportional:

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_13
text: > ```text > Large box: (√210 - √200)² = (14.49 - 14.14)² = 0.12 > Small box: (√30 - √20)² = (5.48 - 4.47)² = 1.02 > ``` > Now the small box error is ~8× larger in the loss → Network learns precision for small objects! > > **Geometric intuition**: √ operation compresses large values more than small values, creating a more balanced loss landscape across different object sizes.

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_14
text: > **Forgetting the Square Root** > > **Mistake**: Predicting w and h directly instead of √w and √h > > **Consequence**: Network struggles to learn small objects accurately. Large objects dominate the loss, making the model biased toward bigger objects. > > **How to spot**: If your model detects large objects well but completely misses small ones, check if you're applying sqrt() to the width and height predictions! > > **In code**: Always use `torch.sqrt(w)` in your target encoding and `torch.square(w_pred)` when converting back. (All Loss Components: /assets/images/yolo/all_losses.png)

id: understanding object detection_1. Localization Loss (Box Regression)_15
text: *Figure: The three components of YOLO loss function - localization (box coordinates), confidence (objectness), and classification (class probabilities)*

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_1
text: 1. Whether an object is present 2. How well the predicted box fits the object

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_2
text: **Formula**:

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_3
text: Where:

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_4

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_5
text: **Two parts**:

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_6
text: 1. **Object cells**: Push confidence toward 1.0 2. **No-object cells**: Push confidence toward 0.0 (but weighted less)

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_7

id: understanding object detection_2. Confidence Loss_8
text: So if predicted box has IOU=0.9 with ground truth, target confidence = 0.9. (Loss Again: /assets/images/yolo/loss_again.png)

id: understanding object detection_3. Classification Loss_0
text: **Goal**: Predict correct class probabilities for cells containing objects.

id: understanding object detection_3. Classification Loss_1
text: **Formula**:

id: understanding object detection_3. Classification Loss_2
text: Where: - `𝟙ᵢᵒᵇʲ` = 1 if cell i contains an object - `pᵢ(c)` = ground truth probability for class c (one-hot: 1 for correct class, 0 otherwise) - `p̂ᵢ(c)` = predicted probability for class c - Sum over all C classes (20 for Pascal VOC)

id: understanding object detection_3. Classification Loss_3
text: **Important**: This loss is **only computed for cells that contain objects**.

id: understanding object detection_3. Classification Loss_4
text: **Example**:

id: understanding object detection_3. Classification Loss_5
text: - Cell contains a person (class 14) - Target: `[0, 0, ..., 1, ..., 0]` (1 at position 14) - Predicted: `[0.1, 0.05, ..., 0.8, ..., 0.02]` - Loss: `Σ(target - pred)² = (0-0.1)² + ... + (1-0.8)² + ... = 0.05`

id: understanding object detection_Training Process with Loss_1
text: 1. Image → Network → Predictions (7×7×30) 2. For each grid cell, compare predictions to targets 3. Compute three loss components 4. Sum weighted losses

id: understanding object detection_Training Process with Loss_2

id: understanding object detection_Training Process with Loss_3
text: **Key insight**: The indicator functions `𝟙ᵢⱼᵒᵇʲ` ensure we only compute loss for relevant predictions:

id: understanding object detection_Training Process with Loss_4

id: understanding object detection_The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)_0
text: So, our model is trained and it's making predictions. How do we know if it's any good? We need a final exam. In object detection, the standard "exam" is called **mAP (mean Average Precision)**.

metadata.section: The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)

id: understanding object detection_The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)_1
text: To understand mAP, we first need to understand two simpler concepts: Precision and Recall.

metadata.section: The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)

id: understanding object detection_The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)_2
text: Imagine our model is taking a test. The test image has 10 dogs in it. The model detects 8 boxes that it claims are dogs.

metadata.section: The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)

id: understanding object detection_The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)_3
text: - Of those 8 boxes, 6 are actually correct (they overlap a real dog with an IOU > 0.5). These are **True Positives(TP)** - The other 2 boxes were mistakes (e.g., it drew a box around a bush). These are **False Positives (FP)** - The model completely missed 4 of the real dogs. These are **False Negatives (FN)**.

metadata.section: The Final Exam: How Do We Grade an Object Detector? (mAP)

id: understanding object detection_Understanding Detection Metrics_0
text: **Three types of predictions:**

id: understanding object detection_Understanding Detection Metrics_1
text: 1. **True Positive (TP)**: Predicted box matches ground truth (IOU ≥ threshold) 2. **False Positive (FP)**: Predicted box doesn't match any ground truth 3. **False Negative (FN)**: Ground truth object that wasn't detected

id: understanding object detection_Precision and Recall_0
text: With these numbers, we can ask two questions:

id: understanding object detection_Precision and Recall_1
text: 1.**Precision: "Of the answers you gave, how many were right?"** - `Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 6 / (6 + 2) = 75%` - This measures how trustworthy the model's predictions are. A high precision model doesn't make many silly mistakes.

id: understanding object detection_Precision and Recall_2
text: 2.**Recall: "Of all the things you *should* have found, how many did you find?"** - `Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 6 / (6 + 4) = 60%` - This measures how comprehensive the model is. A high recall model doesn't miss much.

id: understanding object detection_Precision and Recall_3
text: > The Inevitable Trade-off

id: understanding object detection_Precision and Recall_4
text: There's a constant tug-of-war between precision and recall.

id: understanding object detection_Precision and Recall_5
text: - If you're very timid and only make a prediction when you're 100% sure, you'll have high precision but low recall (you'll miss a lot). - If you're very bold and make tons of guesses, you'll have high recall but low precision (you'll have a lot of junk predictions).

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_0
text: A good model needs to be both precise and comprehensive. To measure this, we can't just look at one point. We need to see how precision and recall change as we adjust our confidence threshold.

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_1
text: **Average Precision (AP)** is a single number that summarizes this trade-off for a *single class* (like "dog"). It's the area under the precision-recall curve. A high AP means the model maintains high precision even as it tries to find more objects (i.e., as recall increases).

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_2
text: **Precision-Recall Curve**: Plot precision vs recall at different confidence thresholds.

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_3
text: **Steps to calculate AP**:

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_4
text: 1. Sort all predictions by confidence 2. For each confidence threshold, compute precision and recall 3. Plot the curve 4. Compute area under curve

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_5
text: **Mean Average Precision (mAP)** is simply the average of the AP scores across all classes. If you have 20 classes, you calculate the AP for dogs, the AP for cats, the AP for cars, and so on, and then average them all together.

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_6
text: This gives us a single, comprehensive number to judge the overall performance of our model. It's the final GPA for our object detector.

id: understanding object detection_So, What is mAP?_7
text: **mAP@0.5**: Use IOU threshold of 0.5 to determine TP **mAP@0.75**: Use IOU threshold of 0.75 (stricter) **mAP@[0.5:0.95]**: Average mAP across IOU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05

text: **Why so fast?**

id: understanding object detection_Speed: Real-Time Detection_3

id: understanding object detection_Accuracy Comparison_0

understanding object detection_Accuracy Comparison_2
