id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_0
text: **Constraint**: Each grid cell can only predict **one object** (despite predicting 2 boxes).

id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_1
text: - Maximum detections: 7×7 = **49 objects** per image

id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_2
text: **Problem**: Fails in crowded scenarios

id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_3
text: - Flocks of birds - Dense crowds - Multiple small objects in one cell

id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_4
text: **Why?** Each cell predicts only **one set of class probabilities**, shared by both boxes.

id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_5
text: **Example failure case**:

id: understanding object detection_1. Limited Objects per Grid Cell_6
text: - Grid cell contains centers of both a dog and bicycle - Cell can only classify as one class - One object will be missed

id: understanding object detection_2. Struggles with Small Objects_0
text: **Problem**: Small objects (especially in groups) are hard to detect.

id: understanding object detection_2. Struggles with Small Objects_1
understanding object detection_2. Struggles with Small Objects_2
text: - 7×7 grid is coarse (each cell = 64×64 pixels) - Small objects may not strongly activate any single cell - Multiple small objects may share a grid cell

id: understanding object detection_2. Struggles with Small Objects_3
text: **Example**: A flock of small birds in the sky.

id: understanding object detection_3. Unusual Aspect Ratios_0
text: **Problem**: Objects with uncommon shapes or aspect ratios are hard to detect.

id: understanding object detection_3. Unusual Aspect Ratios_1
understanding object detection_3. Unusual Aspect Ratios_2
text: - Network learns aspect ratio priors from training data - If training data contains mostly cars that are 2:1 (width:height) - Long, thin cars or unusually shaped objects will be missed

id: understanding object detection_3. Unusual Aspect Ratios_3
text: **Example**: Very long limousine, tall narrow doorway

id: understanding object detection_4. Localization Errors_0
text: **Problem**: Box coordinates are less accurate than two-stage detectors.

id: understanding object detection_4. Localization Errors_1
understanding object detection_4. Localization Errors_2
text: - Coarse feature map (7×7) for final prediction - No iterative refinement (unlike Faster R-CNN) - Especially affects small objects

id: understanding object detection_4. Localization Errors_3
text: **Impact**: Lower IOU values, affects mAP at higher IOU thresholds

id: understanding object detection_5. Box Size Sensitivity_0
text: **Problem**: Despite using √w and √h, small vs large box errors still not perfectly balanced.

id: understanding object detection_5. Box Size Sensitivity_1
text: **Why?** MSE fundamentally treats all errors equally in loss calculation.

id: understanding object detection_6. Class Imbalance Despite Weighting_0
text: **Problem**: Even with λ_noobj = 0.5, "no object" cells still dominate.

id: understanding object detection_6. Class Imbalance Despite Weighting_1
understanding object detection_6. Class Imbalance Despite Weighting_2
text: - Typically 47 cells without objects vs 2-3 with objects - Still creates ~20× more "no object" loss terms

id: understanding object detection_6. Class Imbalance Despite Weighting_3
text: **Impact**:

id: understanding object detection_6. Class Imbalance Despite Weighting_4
text: - Confidence scores may be systematically lower - May miss objects in difficult scenarios

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #1: Small Grouped Objects_0
text: **Why it fails:**

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #1: Small Grouped Objects_1
text: - 7×7 grid = only 49 possible detections maximum - Small birds (5×5 pixels each) → multiple birds share grid cells - Each cell can only detect ONE object (one set of class probs) - Small objects have weak features at 7×7 resolution

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #1: Small Grouped Objects_2
text: **YOLOv3 Fix:** Multi-scale detection (13×13, 26×26, 52×52 grids) → 8,000+ possible detections

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #1: Small Grouped Objects_3
text: **YOLOv10 Fix:** NMS-free detection + multi-scale → perfect for dense small objects

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #2: Unusual Aspect Ratios_0
text: **Why it fails:**

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #2: Unusual Aspect Ratios_1
text: - Training data: mostly ~2:1 aspect ratio cars - Limousine: 10:1 aspect ratio → **out of distribution** - Network hasn't learned to predict such extreme shapes - Two grid cells detect parts separately

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #2: Unusual Aspect Ratios_2
text: **YOLOv2 Fix:** Anchor boxes with multiple aspect ratios (1:1, 1:2, 2:1, 1:3, 3:1)

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #2: Unusual Aspect Ratios_3
text: **YOLOv10 Fix:** Anchor-free design adapts to any shape automatically

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #3: Crowded Scenes_0
text: **Why it fails:**

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #3: Crowded Scenes_1
text: - Hard limit: 7×7 = 49 grid cells - Each cell: only 1 object - Crowded scene: many people share cells - Result: **Systematic undercounting**

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #3: Crowded Scenes_2
text: **YOLOv3 Fix:** Finer grids (52×52 = 2,704 cells) + 3 predictions per cell

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #3: Crowded Scenes_3
text: **YOLOv10 Fix:** No cell limit + NMS-free → handles 100s of objects

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #4: Heavy Occlusion_0
text: **Why it fails:**

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #4: Heavy Occlusion_1
text: - Both object centers fall in same grid cell - YOLO chooses higher confidence box - Occluded object has lower features → lower confidence → ignored

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #4: Heavy Occlusion_2
text: **YOLOv2 Fix:** Multiple anchors per cell → can detect both

id: understanding object detection_Failure Case #4: Heavy Occlusion_3
text: **YOLOv10 Fix:** Dual heads (o2m + o2o) → better occlusion handling

text: | Scenario | YOLOv1 Performance | YOLOv10 Performance | |----------|-------------------|---------------------| | **Small grouped objects** (birds) | 20% recall | 90% recall | | **Unusual aspect ratios** (limousine) | 40% IOU | 85% IOU | | **Crowded scenes** (>50 objects) | 35% recall | 95% recall | | **Heavy occlusion** (overlapping) | 50% recall | 85% recall |

text: > 💡 **Key Takeaway**: YOLOv1 excels at **sparse, medium-sized objects with typical aspect ratios**. For edge cases, use YOLOv3+ or YOLOv10.

id: understanding object detection_The YOLO Family Tree_0
text: YOLOv1 (2016) established the foundation, and subsequent versions addressed its limitations while maintaining the real-time performance philosophy.

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_0
understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_1
text: - **Anchor boxes**: Instead of predicting boxes directly, predict offsets from predefined anchors - **Batch normalization**: Added to all conv layers, improved convergence - **High-resolution classifier**: Pretrain at 448×448 (not 224×224) - **Multi-scale training**: Train on different input sizes - **Better backbone**: Darknet-19 (19 conv layers + 5 maxpool) - **Performance**: 67% mAP at 40 fps, 78.6% mAP at slower speeds

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_2
understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_3
text: - **Multi-scale predictions**: Detect at 3 different scales (better for small objects) - **Better backbone**: Darknet-53 (53 conv layers, residual connections) - **Binary classification**: Use logistic regression instead of softmax (allows multi-label) - **Performance**: 57.9% mAP@0.5, comparable to RetinaNet but 3-4× faster

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_4
understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_5
text: - **Bag of freebies**: Techniques that improve accuracy without increasing inference cost - Data augmentation (Mosaic, MixUp) - Label smoothing - DropBlock regularization - **Bag of specials**: Techniques with small inference cost increase - Mish activation - CSPNet backbone - SPP (Spatial Pyramid Pooling) - PANet neck - **Performance**: 43.5% mAP@0.5:0.95, state-of-the-art at the time

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_6
text: **YOLOv5 - 2020** (Ultralytics):

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_7
text: - **PyTorch implementation**: Easier to use and customize - **Auto-learning anchors**: Automatically cluster anchors from training data - **Model family**: Nano, Small, Medium, Large, XLarge variants - **Better augmentations**: Albumentations integration - **Export options**: ONNX, TensorRT, CoreML, etc.

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_8
text: **YOLOv6, v7, v8 - 2022-2023**: - Various architectural improvements - Better training strategies - Improved backbone designs - Enhanced data augmentation

id: understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_9
understanding object detection_Key Improvements Across Versions_10
text: - **NMS-free detection**: Eliminates need for NMS post-processing - Consistent matching strategy during training - Dual label assignment - Significantly faster inference - **Efficiency optimizations**: - Compact inverted block design - Partial self-attention - Spatial-channel decoupled downsampling - **Model variants**: N/S/M/B/L/X for different speed/accuracy trade-offs - **Performance**: - YOLOv10-X: ~54% mAP@0.5:0.95 on COCO - YOLOv10-N: Real-time on edge devices

id: understanding object detection_Major Paradigm Shifts_0
text: 1. **v1→v2**: Direct prediction → Anchor-based 2. **v2→v3**: Single-scale → Multi-scale detection 3. **v3→v4**: Manual design → Automated architecture search and bag-of-tricks 4. **v4→v5**: Darknet (C) → PyTorch (Python), better tooling 5. **v8→v10**: Anchor-based → Anchor-free, NMS → NMS-free

id: understanding object detection_What Remained Constant_0
text: Despite 10 versions, the core YOLO philosophy persists:

id: understanding object detection_What Remained Constant_1
text: - **Single-stage detection**: One network, one forward pass - **Real-time performance**: Speed is a primary goal - **End-to-end training**: Unified loss function - **Practical focus**: Easy to deploy and use

id: understanding object detection_YOLOv10: Deep Dive into the Latest Version_0
text: YOLOv10 introduces two major innovations: **NMS-free detection** and **holistic efficiency-accuracy driven design**.

metadata.section: YOLOv10: Deep Dive into the Latest Version

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_0
text: **The Problem with NMS:**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_1
text: - Traditional YOLO models generate multiple overlapping boxes per object - Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) is required as post-processing - NMS adds latency and isn't differentiable (can't be optimized end-to-end)

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_2
text: **YOLOv10's Solution: Consistent Dual Label Assignment**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_3
text: YOLOv10 uses **two detection heads** during training:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_4
text: 1. **One-to-Many (o2m) Head**: - Matches each ground truth object with **multiple predictions** - Provides rich supervision signal (explores diverse object locations) - Similar to traditional YOLO training - Analogy: *"I think the cat is here, here, and maybe here"*

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_5
text: 2. **One-to-One (o2o) Head**: - Matches each ground truth object with **exactly one prediction** - Learns to give precise, single predictions - Used during inference (no NMS needed!) - Analogy: *"The cat is exactly here"*

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_6
text: **Consistent Matching Metric:**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_7
text: Both heads use the same scoring formula to match predictions with ground truth:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_8
text: Where:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_9
text: - `spatial_prior` (s): Whether the prediction point lies in/near the GT box (geometric constraint) - `classification_score` (p): Predicted class confidence score - `IOU`: Overlap between predicted and ground truth boxes (localization quality) - `α, β`: Hyperparameters that balance the impact of classification score vs IOU

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_10
text: **Intuition**: The metric `m` scores "how good is this guess" — rewarding predictions that are both the right class (high p) and have good box overlap (high IOU). This ensures both classification accuracy and precise localization matter for matching.

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_11
text: **Why Consistent Matching?**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_12
text: Using the **same metric** on both branches harmonizes the supervision of both heads. If we can align the supervision of the o2o head with that of the o2m head, we can optimize the o2o head toward the direction of o2m head's optimization. As a result, the o2o head provides improved quality samples during inference, leading to better performance.

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_13
text: **Understanding the Supervision Gap:**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_14
text: Both heads produce classification targets, but in different forms:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_15
text: - **o2m** → distributes probability mass across **multiple predictions** (explores diverse locations) - **o2o** → puts all probability mass on a **single prediction** (precise, sharp target)

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_16
text: Naturally, these targets don't look the same — this mismatch is called the **supervision gap**. To measure how "far apart" the two supervision signals are, YOLOv10 uses the **1-Wasserstein distance**:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_17
text: **The Formula**: For denoting an instance's largest IoU as u*, and largest matching scores as m*(o2m) and m*(o2o):

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_18
text: Where:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_19
text: - **First term**: Difference at the shared best prediction index - **Second term**: All leftover o2m mass on other predictions

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_20
text: **Key insight**: By using consistent matching, the best positive sample for the o2m head is also the best for the o2o head. Both heads optimize consistently and harmoniously — the metric ensures you don't need to move much "sand."

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_21
text: By minimizing this gap during training, the o2o head learns to provide **clean, single-box predictions** without needing NMS at inference.

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_22
text: **Training Optimization:**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_23
text: During training, both heads are jointly optimized:

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_24
text: 1. **o2m and o2o metrics** influence label assignments and supervision info for both heads 2. Both use the **consistent matching metric** to find the best matches 3. For o2m: picks multiple answers (predictions p1, p2, p3 boxes) 4. For o2o: picks single best answer (e.g., only p1) 5. Calculate **Wasserstein distance** between top o2m picks and top o2o pick 6. **Minimize loss function** that includes both heads' losses + the supervision gap

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_25
text: **Result**: The o2o head benefits from the rich supervision of o2m (exploring multiple locations) while learning to produce clean, NMS-free single predictions.

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_26
text: **At Inference:**

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_27
text: - Discard the o2m head completely (no extra cost!) - Use only the o2o head → **NMS-free predictions** - Simply pick top-K class scores from [B, N, 4+nc] tensor → done! - For o2o branch, top-1 selection by the same metric (Hungarian matching not needed)

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_28
text: **Dry Run Example**: Detecting a Dog

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_29
text: 1. **Training**: Model learns via o2m/o2o supervision how to score/classify/draw boxes - o2m equation spreads label mass across several positives (exploration) - o2o equation gives sharp target: single o2o positive gets full target, others get zero - Wasserstein distance measures gap between these two distributions

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_30
text: 2. **Inference**: Model outputs raw tensor [B, N, 4+nc] - Preprocessing: Letterbox resize, normalize to [0,1], convert to CHW - Model forward pass: YOLOv10 produces predictions

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_31
text: 3. **Postprocessing** (v10 NMS-free pipeline): - Convert xywh → xyxy bbox format - Scale boxes back to original image (undo letterbox padding) - Pick top-K class scores from [N, 4+nc] predictions - No NMS needed! Just filter by confidence threshold

id: understanding object detection_1. NMS-Free Training with Dual Heads_32
text: 4. **Final Result**: Clean detection with one strong prediction per object - Dog box + label, no duplicate messy boxes - 40% faster than YOLOv8 (no NMS overhead)

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_0
text: **A. Lightweight Classification Head**

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_1
text: **Observation**: In YOLOv8:

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_2
text: - Classification head: 5.95G FLOPs, 1.51M params - Regression head: 2.34G FLOPs, 0.64M params - Classification is **2.5× heavier** despite regression being more important for accuracy!

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_3
text: **Solution**: Redesign classification head using:

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_4
text: - Two **depthwise separable 3×3 convolutions** (cheap spatial learning) - One **1×1 convolution** (channel mixing) - Result: Significantly lower computational cost while maintaining performance

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_5
text: **B. Spatial-Channel Decoupled Downsampling**

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_6
text: **Traditional Approach**: Single 3×3 conv with stride=2 does both:

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_7
text: - Spatial reduction: H×W → H/2×W/2 - Channel increase: C → 2C - Cost: **O(9/2 × H×W×C²)** — expensive!

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_8
text: **YOLOv10 Approach**: Decouple the operations:

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_9
text: 1. **Pointwise conv (1×1)**: Only changes channels (C → 2C) 2. **Depthwise conv (3×3, stride=2)**: Only reduces spatial dimensions

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_10
text: - New cost: **O(2×H×W×C² + 9/2×H×W×C)** — much cheaper!

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_11
text: **C. Rank-Guided Block Design**

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_12
text: **The Problem**: Not all network stages are equally important — some are redundant.

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_13
text: **The Solution**:

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_14
text: 1. Compute **intrinsic rank** of each stage's last convolution (using SVD) 2. Sort stages from lowest rank (most redundant) to highest 3. Replace redundant stages with **Compact Inverted Blocks (CIB)**: - Depthwise convs for efficient spatial mixing - Pointwise convs for cheap channel mixing - Much lighter than standard bottleneck blocks 4. Keep high-rank (important) stages strong

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_15
text: **For important (high-rank) stages**:

id: understanding object detection_2. Architectural Innovations_16
text: - Use **7×7 large kernel convolutions** in deeper layers (bigger receptive field) - Apply **Partial Self-Attention (PSA)** to half the channels (global context at low cost)

id: understanding object detection_3. Enhanced Backbone: CSPNet_0
text: **CSP (Cross-Stage Partial) Network** builds on DenseNet:

id: understanding object detection_3. Enhanced Backbone: CSPNet_1
text: **DenseNet**: Each layer concatenates all previous layers:

id: understanding object detection_3. Enhanced Backbone: CSPNet_2
text: **CSPNet**: Separates feature map into two parts:

id: understanding object detection_3. Enhanced Backbone: CSPNet_3
text: - Part 1: Goes through dense block + transition layer - Part 2: Bypassed and combined later - Reduces computation while maintaining rich feature representation

id: understanding object detection_4. Performance Results on big dataset_6
text: **Why the Improvement?**

id: understanding object detection_4. Performance Results on big dataset_7
text: 1. **NMS-free**: Eliminates post-processing latency 2. **Efficient architecture**: Lighter heads, decoupled downsampling 3. **Better supervision**: Dual-head training with consistent matching 4. **Optimized blocks**: CIB for redundant stages, large kernels + PSA for important stages

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_0
text: **Model Export:**

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_1
text: - Best model: `best.pt` (PyTorch weights) - Converted to ONNX for production deployment - Custom preprocessing: Ultralytics letterbox (aspect ratio preserved, padded to stride=32) - Custom postprocessing: `postprocess_nms_free` (top-K filtering, box scaling)

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_2
text: **Inference Pipeline:**

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_3
text: 1. **Input**: RGB image from RTSP stream (any size)

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_4
text: 2. **Preprocessing** (Ultralytics letterbox): - Keep aspect ratio, pad to multiple of stride=32 - Convert to RGB, scale to [0,1] - Convert to CHW format (channels first) - Returns image tensor + scale factor + padding values (for later box mapping)

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_5
text: 3. **Model Forward Pass**: - YOLOv10m processes image - Output: tensor of shape **[B, N, 4+nc]** or **[B, 4+nc, N]** - Where: B=batch, N=number of predictions, nc=number of classes - Boxes in xywh format (center x, center y, width, height - all scaled) - Scores are per-class probabilities

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_6
text: 4. **Postprocessing** (`postprocess_nms_free` function): - **Accept both layouts**: [B, N, 4+nc] or [B, 4+nc, N] (works for NumPy arrays) - **xywh → xyxy conversion**: Convert center format to corner format - **scale_boxes**: Undo letterbox transform (subtract pad, divide by ratio, clip to bounds) - **Top-K filtering**: Select predictions with highest class scores - **No NMS needed** — one prediction per object by design! - Returns: List of dicts per image `{boxes: [M,4], scores: [M], labels: [M]}`

id: understanding object detection_5. Deployment_7
text: 5. **Output**: Clean detections ready for visualization/downstream use

id: understanding object detection_Conclusion: The Legacy of "You Only Look Once"_0
text: YOLOv1 was more than just a model; it was a philosophical shift. It taught the world that object detection could be framed as a single, elegant regression problem. It prioritized speed and simplicity, opening the door to applications that were previously unimaginable.

metadata.section: Conclusion: The Legacy of "You Only Look Once"

id: understanding object detection_Conclusion: The Legacy of "You Only Look Once"_1
text: From the clunky but brilliant v1 to the sleek, end-to-end v10, the journey of YOLO is a perfect story of scientific progress: a great idea, honestly acknowledged limitations, and a decade of relentless, community-driven effort to build something better. The next time you see a self-driving car navigate a busy street, you'll know it stands on the shoulders of a giant—an idea that dared to just look once.

metadata.section: Conclusion: The Legacy of "You Only Look Once"

text: **What YOLOv1 proved:**

metadata.section: Conclusion: The Legacy of "You Only Look Once"

id: understanding object detection_Conclusion: The Legacy of "You Only Look Once"_4
text: While YOLOv1 had limitations (small objects, crowded scenes, unusual aspect ratios), it established the foundation for a family of detectors that continues to push the boundaries of speed and accuracy.

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_4

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_5
text: **c. Loss Calculation**

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_6
text: - Box loss (7.5x weight): IoU/GIoU loss for bbox coordinates - Class loss (1.5x weight): Binary cross-entropy for classification - DFL loss (1.5x weight): Distribution focal loss for bbox refinement - Total loss = weighted sum of above

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_7
text: > **What do these mean?**

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_8
text: > - **Box loss**: How well the model draws a box around the phone > - **Class loss**: How sure the model is that the thing is a phone > - **DFL loss**: How precisely the model guesses the edges of the box

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_9
text: **d. Backward Pass**

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_10
text: - Calculate gradients using total loss - Backpropagation and updating of gradients using Optimiser (I used AdamW with momentum)

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_11
text: **e. Optimizer Step (AdamW)**

id: understanding object detection_1. Training_12
text: - Update weights using gradients - Apply learning rate (starts at 0.0005, decays to 0.01 × lr0) - Apply weight decay (0.0005) for regularization - Apply momentum (0.9)

text: After all training batches:

id: understanding object detection_2. Validation (every epoch)_1
text: **a. Switch to eval mode**

id: understanding object detection_2. Validation (every epoch)_2
text: - Disable dropout (full model instead of skipping some layers) - Use batch normalization in eval mode (already learned features instead of learning new ones) - No augmentations (no flips)

id: understanding object detection_2. Validation (every epoch)_3
text: **b. For each validation image**

id: understanding object detection_2. Validation (every epoch)_4
text: - Forward pass (no gradient calculation) - Get predictions with conf threshold (default 0.001 for val) - Apply NMS (non-maximum suppression: if the model draws many boxes on the same phone, keep only the best one and throw away the rest) with IoU threshold 0.45

id: understanding object detection_2. Validation (every epoch)_5
text: **c. Metric Calculation**

id: understanding object detection_2. Validation (every epoch)_6
text: - Match predictions to ground truth (IoU >= 0.5) - Calculate per-class metrics: - Precision = TP / (TP + FP) - Recall = TP / (TP + FN) - mAP@50 = mean AP at IoU=0.5 - mAP@50-95 = mean AP averaged over IoU 0.5 to 0.95 - Calculate overall metrics (averaged across all classes) (You can see how CNN works here: https://cs231n.stanford.edu/) (PyTorch implementation of YOLOV1 paper: https://github.com/samitmohan/YOLOv1) (Intro to YOLO: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lcArnTfpPBM)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_0
text: How objects are converted into vectors? Let's say you have a PDF file (consisting of for all textual documents)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_1
text: How do you describe it's properties to a computer that only understands math? Through numbers

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_2
text: Look at every document and plot it in 2D space

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_3
text: X axis -> length of document

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_4
text: Y axis -> how real the document is (fictional, non fictional)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_5
text: [File] -> [2.6, 3.5, 1.5, 8.2, 6.7] (Spatial Domain) (2DSpace Image: /assets/images/ai/vector_doc_novels.png)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_6
text: We converted meaning of document -> topological space

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_7
text: Problem? 2D isn't enough to represent all our data

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_8
text: Let's say we take a 3rd dimension -> popularity, 4th dimension -> year it was written in etc..

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_9
text: We end up with infinite number of dimensions to represent every single document..

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_10
text: - Constraint on the number of dimensions (D) (LLAMA (language model by Meta)-> 4096)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_11
text: How to map infinitely complex object -> fixed number of documents? Compression?

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_12
text: **Sounds like something neural networks do..** (Neural Network: /assets/images/ai/NN.png) (TexttoVec: /assets/images/ai/vector1D.png)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_13
text: So 100 documents will have 100 vectors -> which can be represented in a n-dimensional space.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_14
text: Vectors closer to other vectors will be nearby in the space:

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_15
text: - Harry Potter & Dan Brown docs near each other - Research papers are near one another, and so on...

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_16
text: Similar objects will have similar/nearby distance ( (Euclidean distance: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_17
text: ) to each other.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_18
text: So if two objects which are similar are nearby -> you reward the model else you penalise it.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_19
text: **What do we mean by "reward" and "penalise" here?**

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_20
text: This works on Backpropagation

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_21
text: - We want predicted output = actual output so we define a loss function and our goal is to minimise that loss function *hint: calculus*, think of standing on the edge of a bowl and you want to get to the bottom of the bowl -> you take baby steps until you get to the extreme minimum point of the bowl - More on this in my (blog: https://samitmohan.github.io/tech/2025/10/25/nn.html)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_22
text: Hence the model learns what object are close to each other & what objects are far away when it comes to similarity, look up this beautiful blog on ( (vecotr embeddings: https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-word2vec/)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_23
text: ) for more.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_24
text: > **Key Concept:** Vector embeddings compress infinite complexity into fixed dimensions while preserving semantic similarity. Objects that are semantically similar (Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings) will have nearby vectors in the embedding space, enabling efficient similarity search through distance calculations.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_25
text: > Sidenote: how are we penalising the output? Gradient Change (explained below)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_26
text: *Penalty*

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_27
text: When the model makes a mistake—for example, it calculates that a Harry Potter book is similar to a quantum physics paper—we don't literally "punish" it. Instead, we have a mathematical function called a **Loss Function**. This function measures how far off the model's prediction is from the actual, desired output.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_28
text: If two dissimilar objects are close together in the vector space, the loss function will produce a high value. This high value is the "penalty." (Incorrect State: /assets/images/ai/incorrect_state.png)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_29
text: **The red dot is incorrectly placed near the blue cluster, resulting in a large error or "penalty".**

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_30
text: Now, how do we use this penalty to fix the model? This is where backpropagation and gradient descent come in.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_31
text: - Backpropagation calculates the gradient of the loss function. The gradient is a vector that points in the direction of the steepest increase in the loss.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_32
text: - Gradient Descent takes this gradient and moves the model's weights (the numbers that determine the vector positions) in the opposite direction. This is the direction of the steepest decrease in loss.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_33
text: Think of it like a ball rolling down a hill. The gradient tells you which way is "up," so you move the ball "down" to get to the bottom of the valley (the minimum loss).

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_34
text: The following image visualizes this process on a loss surface: (Gradient Change: /assets/images/ai/gradient_change.png)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_35
text: *Figure 1.1: Gradient descent optimization navigates the loss surface by moving in the direction of steepest descent, iteratively updating weights until reaching the minimum loss.*

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_36
text: Conversely, "rewarding" the model simply means that when it gets a prediction right (e.g., placing Harry Potter near Dan Brown), the loss function produces a low value.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_37
text: In this case, the gradient will be very small, meaning the weights won't change much.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_38
text: The model is effectively told, "You're doing great, keep doing what you're doing." (Correct State: /assets/images/ai/correct_state.png)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_39
text: **The red dot has moved to its correct position. The loss is now low, and the gradient is small.**

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_40
text: This cycle of calculating loss, determining the gradient, and updating weights is repeated millions of times during training, allowing the model to learn the complex relationships between objects in its n-dimensional space

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_41
text: Once you have these vector embeddings of similar words being nearby, you can do fun stuff with it.

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_42
text: **Example** -> If you have man and woman (which are obviously nearby in this space) and you have plotted the point king in this same dimension, you can quickly do king - man + woman to get a NEW word -> queen

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_43
text: *Illustrations of how nearby objects relate* (PE: /assets/images/ai/man_king.png) (King+man: /assets/images/ai/kingman.png) (KingMan2: /assets/images/ai/uncleaunt.png)

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_44
text: **Summary:**

id: AI engineering_How are vectors constructed_45
text: - Vector is an ordered array of numerical values representing features/data points/parameters in a multi-dimensional space - Similar objects generate vectors such that they are closer when plotted in this space - Train baseline model/neural network using loss functions OR (fine-tune: https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/fine-tuning-large-language-models)

text: **Core Concepts:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 1: Key Takeaways_2
text: - **Vectors compress infinite complexity into fixed dimensions**: A complex document becomes a point in 4096-dimensional space - **Similar objects cluster together**: Harry Potter and Lord of the Rings will have nearby vectors; quantum physics papers will be far away - **Training uses gradient descent**: The model learns through backpropagation, adjusting weights to minimize the loss function

id: AI engineering_Chapter 1: Key Takeaways_4

id: AI engineering_Chapter 1: Key Takeaways_5

id: AI engineering_Chapter 1: Key Takeaways_6

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_0
text: Vector databases deal with multiple dimensions. Sorting across all dimensions is not possible. Binary search cannot be applied in a high-dimensional vector space.

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_1
text: Instead, vector databases use specialized techniques to find approximate nearest neighbors. This includes building spatial partitioning structures like HNSW or IVF.

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_2
text: K-D tree: allows search in k-dimensional space (what we need)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_3
text: Can split trees based on different dimensions, works same as BST if you have taken an algorithms class. (KDTree: /assets/images/ai/kdTree.png)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_4
text: **Drawback:** space (lots of branching) + not accurate (root is heavily branched) (More on KD-Trees: https://medium.com/@katyayanivemula90/what-is-a-k-dimensional-tree-8265cc737d77)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_5
text: *HNSW*: Hierarichal Navigable Small Worlds

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_6
text: - Every vector is connected to the k-nearest points to it. (Outliers are connected to some points, center vectors (popular) are connected to all other vectors) - Popular vectors are advanced to next level (fewer vectors that are good representaiton of underlying space)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_7
text: Query hits the root -> finds nearby vector to root, if found -> OK, else you go deeper into the layer. (HNSW2: /assets/images/ai/HNSW.png) (HNSW: /assets/images/ai/HNSW2.png)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_8
text: *Figure 2.2: HNSW search process - query navigates from top layer through increasingly dense layers until finding nearest neighbors.*

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_9
text: **Drawback**:Large scale: doesn't work,

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_10
text: *So what does work?*

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_11
text: - Inverted File Index; doc vectors -> clusters (kmeans) -> each cluster has a centroid - Find nearest centroid to that query (input query) :: Search k nearest clusters

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_12
text: **IVF (Inverted File)** is GPU-friendly because it allows for efficient parallel processing of large datasets, leveraging the massive parallelism of GPUs for fast indexing and retrieval. In contrast, HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is CPU-friendly as it relies on graph-based structures that typically perform better on CPUs due to their lower memory overhead and better cache utilization during nearest neighbor searches. (IFI: /assets/images/ai/IVI2.png)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_13
text: In IVF (Inverted File Index), distance is first calculated based on the centroid closest to the query vector and not the actual vector points themselves. This means the search might miss the true nearest neighbor if it falls into a different cluster. As a result, IVF can return a point that's actually farther from the query in real vector space. (IFI2: /assets/images/ai/IVI.png)

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_14
text: Increasing the number of clusters improves accuracy: with more clusters, the chances are higher that the actual closest point to the query ends up in a nearby or selected cluster, leading to better search results.

id: AI engineering_Vector Search?_15
text: Search query vector can fail when closest point to query is assigned to centroid further than the nearest centroid.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_0
text: We've explored the specialized world of vector databases and why they're essential for AI systems. Here's what matters:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_1
text: **Core Concepts:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_2
text: - **Vector databases optimize for similarity search, not ACID properties**: Unlike traditional databases, they trade consistency for speed - **Compression is crucial**: Product Quantization and Scalar Quantization reduce memory footprint by 32-64x with minimal accuracy loss - **Search algorithms enable sub-linear performance**: HNSW (graph-based) and IVF (clustering-based) make billion-vector search practical - **Production systems use specialized architectures**: Milvus, pgVector, and others provide distributed, scalable vector storage

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_3
text: **Key Trade-offs:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_4
text: - **Memory vs Accuracy**: Compression saves space but introduces quantization errors - **Speed vs Recall**: Approximate nearest neighbor algorithms are fast but may miss some relevant results - **CPU vs GPU**: HNSW works well on CPUs; IVF leverages GPU parallelism

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_5
text: **Why This Matters:** Vector databases are the infrastructure layer that makes modern AI applications possible - from semantic search to RAG pipelines to recommendation systems. Without efficient vector storage and retrieval, LLMs would be much less useful.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_6
text: **Next Steps:** Now that we understand how vectors are created (Chapter 1) and stored/searched (Chapter 2), we need to understand how text becomes vectors in the first place. That's where tokenization comes in - the crucial preprocessing step that bridges human language and machine learning.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 2: Key Takeaways_7
AI engineering_Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers_0
text: Before we dive into how LLMs work, we need to understand a fundamental preprocessing step: **tokenization**.

metadata.section: Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers_1
text: Neural networks can't process raw text - they need numbers. But how do we convert "Hello, world!" into something a computer can compute with?

metadata.section: Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers_2
text: The answer isn't as simple as assigning each character a number. Modern tokenization algorithms strike a balance between efficiency (small vocabulary size) and meaning preservation (keeping word boundaries intact).

metadata.section: Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Tokenization - From Text to Numbers_3
text: This chapter explores how tokenization works and why it's crucial for LLM performance. (Tokenisation Image: /assets/images/ai/nnTokensation.png) (Tokensiation2: /assets/images/ai/tokenisation_for_blog.png) (Real Time Demonstration of Tokenisation: https://tiktokenizer.vercel.app/)

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_0
text: "I love you" → embeddings "You love I" → same embeddings, different meaning

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_1
text: Transformers have no idea about sequence order by default.add position information into the input vectors.

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_2
text: input_to_transformer = word_embedding + positional_encoding

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_3
text: Each position number (0, 1, 2, 3… ) is converted into a bunch of sine/cos waves:

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_4
text: Long waves capture coarse position

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_5
text: Short waves capture fine position

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_6
text: Mixed waves uniquely identify every position

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_7
text: Imagine this as using multiple clock hands rotating at different speeds — each timestamp combination is unique.

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_8
text: For a position pos and dimension i:: $$ \text{PE}[pos,\; 2i] = \sin\!\left( \frac{pos}{10000^{\,i / d_{\text{model}}}} \right) $$

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_9
text: $$ \text{PE}[pos,\; 2i+1] = \cos\!\left( \frac{pos}{10000^{\,i / d_{\text{model}}}} \right) $$

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_10
text: (Even indices: sine, Odd indices: cosine)

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_11
text: Have different meanings beacuse the position of why is different hence we add positional encodings to the input vector/token so model knows where the word actually is. (PE: /assets/images/ai/pe.png)

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_12
text: *Code for positional encodings*

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_13
text: Each token ID indexes into the embedding matrix, retrieving its corresponding embedding vector. If the model has 4096 dimensions, each token becomes a vector of 4096 floating-point numbers.

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_14
text: > programming section

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_15
text: **Q. Implementing BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) from Scratch**

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_16
text: **How this works:**

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_17
text: 1. Start with individual characters as tokens 2. Find the most frequent adjacent pair 3. Merge that pair into a new token 4. Repeat for num_merges iterations 5. Apply learned merges to new text

id: AI engineering_Positional Embeddings_18
text: This is the same algorithm GPT and other modern LLMs use for tokenization!

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_0
text: We've explored how raw text is transformed into numerical representations that neural networks can process:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_1
text: **Core Concepts:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_2
text: - **Tokenization bridges text and ML**: Cannot feed raw strings to neural networks; need numerical representations - **BPE strikes the optimal balance**: Not too granular (characters) nor too coarse (words); subword tokenization handles rare words and multiple languages - **Token IDs map to embeddings**: Each token becomes a high-dimensional vector (typically 768-4096 dimensions) - **Efficiency matters**: Fewer tokens = less computation = faster inference and lower costs

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_3
text: **Key Insight:** Tokenization is not just preprocessing - it's a core architectural decision that affects:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_4
text: - Vocabulary size (directly impacts model size) - Multilingual capability (BPE handles character-level patterns) - Cost and speed (more tokens = more money and time)

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_5
text: **Why This Matters:** Every interaction with an LLM begins with tokenization. Understanding it helps you:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_6
text: - Optimize prompts (stay under context limits) - Debug weird model behavior (check how your text is tokenized) - Estimate costs (tokens are the billing unit for API calls)

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_7
text: **Next Steps:** Now that we understand how text becomes tokens, and tokens become vectors, we're ready to explore the heart of modern AI: the **Transformer architecture**.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_8
text: Transformers use self-attention to let every token "look at" every other token, enabling context-aware understanding that makes LLMs so powerful.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 3: Key Takeaways_9
AI engineering_LLM Internals_0
text: > How do these LLMs work?

id: AI engineering_LLM Internals_1
text: Transformers are the architecture that powers GPT, BERT, LLaMA, and virtually every modern LLM. At their core, they perform two key operations per layer:

id: AI engineering_LLM Internals_2
text: 1. **Multi-head self-attention**: Lets tokens understand their relationship to other tokens (lets you know how one token or word is related to another) 2. **Feed-forward networks**: Transforms representations to minimize prediction error (helps minimise the Loss Function so your predicted text = ground truth(for example if you ask "What is state of water" The prediction will try to be solid, liquid, and gaseous as accurately as it can (which is the ground truth given during training))

id: AI engineering_LLM Internals_3
text: Doing enough of this ground truth and prediction during training makes model good enough to come up with it's own answer based on training on all of text on the internet and hence can perform extremely well during inference time when asked new questions.

id: AI engineering_LLM Internals_4
text: Through stacking many layers (GPT-3 has 96!), the model progressively builds richer representations until it can predict what comes next with remarkable accuracy.

id: AI engineering_LLM Internals_5
text: Let's break down how this works, starting with the fundamental mechanism: **attention**.

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_0
text: When we read a sentence, we don’t understand each word in isolation — we look at the surrounding words to figure out what each word means.

metadata.section: Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_1
text: **For example:**

metadata.section: Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_2
text: “The crane flew away.” → You think of a **bird.**

metadata.section: Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_3
text: “The crane lifted a car.” → You think of a **machine.**

metadata.section: Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_4
text: This is what attention allows AI models to do. It lets them focus on relevant parts of the sentence to understand what a word or token really means in context.

metadata.section: Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_5
text: *In transformers, this is called self-attention.*

metadata.section: Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)

id: AI engineering_Self Attention Mechanism (how one word relates to itself and others)_6
text: Every word looks at every other word in the sentence and decides how important each one is. That importance is then used to build a richer, more meaningful representation of the word — one that captures its role in the full sentence. (Crane: /assets/images/ai/crane.png) (Cran2: /assets/images/ai/crane2.png) (crane3: /assets/images/ai/crane_arm.png)

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_0
text: - Query: What is my question (What is the highest salary of Software Engineer) - Key: What is the parameter for my question (in Microsoft) - Value: What is my answer (300k+ (lol))

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_1
text: - Query: what the current token is looking for e.g. a vowel may be looking for a consonant (in the case of character-level tokenization), a noun may be looking for verbs associated with it etc. - Key: what I can offer i.e. what response a token offers for a query, what a token is (I am a verb, an adjective...) - Value: forementioned matrices that encompasses the context, meaning and weight of each token (e.g. token 2 is valuable in predicting tokens 10, 15; token 2 has such an embedding, carries such weight in predicting tokens x and y...)

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_2
text: - Query: Spotlight projector - Key: Shifting of spotlight from one place to another - Value: When I shine the spotlight on a particular screen, what do I see?

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_3
text: Query tells you **which word you're seeing attention for** and keys tell you **how much that word affects this incoming word by** (crane affected by wings but not by the word THE)... Then a matrix is formed between Query and Key by multiplying them:: dot_product(Q, K) for all words. (beautiful blog on construction of Q, K, V matrices: https://arpitbhayani.me/blogs/qkv-matrices)

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_4

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_6

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_7
text: This is how the model knows what english words mean and how it can figure out the meaning of the input text.

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_8
text: **Attention mechanism:** how much every word / token should attend to every other word / token.

id: AI engineering_Some analogies for Q,K,V matrices_9

text: > **Common Mistake:** Forgetting to scale attention scores by √d_k leads to numerical instability. Without scaling, dot products can grow very large (e.g., 100+), pushing softmax into regions with near-zero gradients (vanishing gradient problem). This causes training instability and the model fails to learn long-range dependencies.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_0
text: **Step 1:** Tokenization.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_1
text: **Step 2:** Embedding lookup. Each token ID indexes into the embedding matrix, retrieving its corresponding embedding vector. If the model has 4096 dimensions, each token becomes a vector of 4096 floating-point numbers.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_2
text: **Step 3:** Add positional encodings

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_3
text: **Step 4:** The input embeddings flow through each transformer layer. For a 32-layer model, this happens 32 times.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_4
text: **Step 5:** Generate first token. After the final layer, the hidden states get projected to vocabulary size through a linear layer, then softmax converts these logits to probabilities over all possible next tokens.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_5
text: **Step 6:** Decode phase. Now we generate tokens one at a time. For each new token, we only compute fresh Q, K, V for that token, retrieving cached values for all previous tokens.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_6
text: **Step 7:** Detokenization. Finally, the sequence of token IDs gets converted back to text using the tokenizer’s vocabulary. output_text = tokenizer.decode(generated_tokens)

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_7
text: This entire process repeats for every token generated, with the KV cache growing at each step. The decode phase continues until the model generates a stop token or reaches a maximum length limit.

id: AI engineering_Recap: From Internet to ChatGPT_8
text: Now that we understand the transformer architecture, let's see **how a model like ChatGPT is actually created, from raw data to production assistant.**

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_0
text: **Download and preprocess the internet**

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_1
text: - Scrape text from web pages, books, papers, code repositories - Clean and deduplicate data - Tools: (FineWeb: https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceFW/blogpost-fineweb-v1)

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_2
text: for large-scale data

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_3

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_4
text: - Convert text → sequence of tokens using BPE - Start with 256 byte-level tokens - Iteratively merge most common pairs - Visualize: (TikTokenizer: https://tiktokenizer.vercel.app/)

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_5
text: **Neural Network Training**

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_6
text: - Input: Sequence of tokens - Process: Transformer layers (attention + FFN) - Loss: Predict next token correctly - Backpropagation tunes weights and biases - Train for weeks/months on thousands of GPUs (NN Training Flow: /assets/images/ai/neural-net-training-karpathy.png) (Black Box NN: /assets/images/ai/black_box_neural_network.png)

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_7
text: **Inference/Prediction**

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_8
text: - Predict one token at a time - Generate probability distribution over vocabulary - "Hi my name is Samit and this website is my home on the _" - internet: 90% - web: 8% - blog: 2% - Sample from distribution (temperature controls randomness)

id: AI engineering_Step 1: Pre-Training (Building the Base Model)_9
text: **Result:** A "base model" - an internet document simulator that can continue text, but doesn't follow instructions or avoid harmful outputs.

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_0
text: The base model needs alignment with human values and instruction-following capability.

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_1
text: **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_2
text: - Human labelers write example conversations - Model learns to respond to instructions rather than just continue text - Think: Base model = theory, SFT = worked examples - Today: Much of this is LLM-assisted (humans edit AI-generated responses)

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_3
text: **Challenges the base model has:**

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_4
text: - Can't count accurately - Poor spelling (sees tokens, not letters) - Needs tools for math/code execution - May hallucinate facts (Hallucinations: /assets/images/ai/hallucinations.png)

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_5
text: **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)**

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_6
text: - Generate multiple responses for each query - Humans rank them (A vs B comparisons) - Train a reward model to predict human preferences - Use PPO to optimize the LLM toward high-reward outputs (Emily Apple Example: /assets/images/ai/emily_apple_example.png)

id: AI engineering_Step 2: Post-Training (Making It Useful & Safe)_7
text: **Result:** A helpful, harmless, honest assistant that follows instructions, uses tools when needed, and aligns with human preferences.

text: **How to improve these models?** Models are better at evaluating than generating, so whatever answer you get goes back to the model to evaluate if this is correct or not.

id: AI engineering_Training Beyond Next-Token Prediction: Reasoning & Alignment_0
text: So far we've covered how transformers work architecturally - but modern LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude don't just predict the next token. They reason, follow instructions, and avoid harmful outputs. How?

metadata.section: Training Beyond Next-Token Prediction: Reasoning & Alignment

id: AI engineering_The Reasoning Challenge_0
text: Language models are fundamentally pattern matchers trained on text prediction. They excel at memorization but struggle with true reasoning. Consider a chess engine:

id: AI engineering_The Reasoning Challenge_1
text: The model can memorize millions of chess games, but when faced with a novel position, it can't "think" about strategy - it doesn't understand the physics of the game or have a goal (winning). It just pattern-matches similar positions it's seen before.

id: AI engineering_The Reasoning Challenge_2
text: **The question:** How do we teach models to reason?

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_0
text: We can't build true logical reasoning (if we could, we'd have AGI!), but we can **simulate reasoning behavior** through reinforcement learning.

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_1
text: **The chess analogy:** Imagine teaching a model chess by giving it rewards:

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_2
text: - Checkmate in 2 moves → +100 points - Checkmate in 4 moves → 0 points - Checkmate in 6 moves → -100 points (Checkmate Rewards: /assets/images/ai/checkmate_RF.png) (Checkmate Moves: /assets/images/ai/Checkmate.png)

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_3
text: The model learns to navigate the "search space" of possible moves, preferring paths that lead to better outcomes. This is reinforcement learning.

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_4
text: **Applying RLHF to LLMs:**

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_5
text: For LLMs, we can't give numeric rewards directly. Instead:

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_6
text: 1. Generate multiple responses to a query 2. Have humans rank them ("Which is better: Option A or Option B?") 3. Train a **reward model** to predict human preferences 4. Use reinforcement learning to steer the LLM toward high-reward outputs

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_7
text: **Example:**

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_8
text: - Query: "Write a blog post about AI" - LLM generates 5 different blog posts - Humans pick the best one - Model learns what makes a "good" blog post (Policy Optimization: /assets/images/ai/policy.png)

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_9
text: **PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization):** Human feedback is expensive and noisy. PPO solves this by taking small, conservative policy updates. Think of it like gradient descent for decision-making:

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_10
text: - If one response got +100 reward, nearby responses likely get +99, +98, etc. - The model learns a smooth reward landscape from sparse human feedback - Small steps prevent catastrophic forgetting

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_11
text: **Limitations:**

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

id: AI engineering_RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback_12
text: - Humans aren't perfect evaluators (that's why ChatGPT uses pairwise comparisons, not scoring) - Human feedback is expensive to collect at scale - Sometimes humans disagree or give malicious feedback

metadata.section: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
