id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_0
text: We've explored the complete picture of modern LLMs - from architecture to reasoning. Here's what you need to remember:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_1
text: **Core Architecture:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_2
text: - **Self-attention enables context-aware understanding**: Every token can "look at" every other token through Q/K/V matrices - **Multi-head attention captures different relationships**: Different heads learn syntax, semantics, long-range dependencies - **Positional encodings preserve order**: Sinusoidal functions tell the model where each token sits in the sequence - **Causal masking prevents cheating**: During training, token i can only see tokens 0 through i-1, not future tokens - **Layer stacking builds abstraction**: Each transformer layer builds higher-level representations (96 layers in GPT-3)

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_3
text: **Making Models Smart (RLHF & Reasoning):**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_4
text: - **RLHF aligns models with human preferences**: Reward models + reinforcement learning steer outputs toward quality - **Chain of Thought (CoT) teaches step-by-step reasoning**: Models learn to show their work, not just answer - **Tree of Thought (ToT) explores multiple paths**: Like MCTS, explores and prunes reasoning branches - **Tool usage extends capabilities**: LLMs call calculators, APIs, and code interpreters when needed

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_5
text: **The Complete Flow:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_6
text: 1. Text → Tokens → Token embeddings 2. Add positional encodings 3. Pass through N transformer layers (attention + FFN + residual connections) 4. Final layer outputs probability distribution over vocabulary 5. Apply temperature sampling to pick next token 6. If tool needed → call external API → incorporate result 7. Repeat until completion

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_7
text: **Why This Matters:** Understanding transformers AND training techniques helps you:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_8
text: - **Debug model behavior**: Know why context window matters, how attention patterns form - **Optimize prompts**: Use CoT prompting, leverage tool calling effectively - **Architect systems**: Choose model size, layer count, attention heads based on task requirements - **Fine-tune effectively**: Understand what RLHF can and can't fix

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_9
text: **The Performance Problem:** There's a catch: transformer inference is **slow**. Each new token requires attending to all previous tokens, making generation quadratic in sequence length. For long contexts (32k+ tokens), this becomes prohibitively expensive.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 4: Key Takeaways_10
text: **Next Steps:** Now that we understand how transformers work, we need to make them **fast**. Chapter 5 covers the cutting-edge optimization techniques that make production LLMs practical: KV caching, flash attention, quantization, and more.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast_0
text: The transformer architecture is elegant but computationally expensive. Generating a single response can require billions of matrix operations. For production systems serving thousands of users, optimization isn't optional - it's existential.

metadata.section: Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast_1
text: This chapter covers the key techniques that make modern LLMs practical:

metadata.section: Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast_2
text: - **KV caching**: Avoid recomputing attention for past tokens (reduces O(n²) to O(n)) - **Flash attention**: Optimize memory bandwidth through tiling - **Quantization**: Reduce precision (FP32 → INT8) for 4x speedup - **Paged attention**: Efficient memory management for variable-length sequences

metadata.section: Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast_3
text: Let's start with the most impactful optimization: **KV caching**.

metadata.section: Chapter 5: Inference Optimization - Making LLMs Fast

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_0
text: In Transformers, the model prcesses input tokens in parallel (computes Q,K,V for each token) making sure all tokens can see all other tokens (input) and compute attention score for every pair of position.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_1
text: Decoder phase starts and model produces tokens one at a time, each new token is based on all previous tokens BUT only latest token needs fresh Q,K,V computations (Q,K,V doesn't get computed for all previous tokens (that will be a huge complexity of matrix multiplications over and over again when we have already calculated it beforehand (solution to this -> store them in a cache {KV Cache}))

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_2
text: **KV Caching & Attention Optimization: From O(n²) to O(n)**

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_3
text: *KV caching stores previously computed attention keys and values, avoiding recomputation and reducing complexity from O(n²) to O(n) for autoregressive generation.*

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_4
text: Let's say you're using a language model to generate a sentence, one word at a time.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_5
text: At every step, the model runs the attention mechanism for all the words until now.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_6
text: **Example**: I … (1 x 1 attention matrix)

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_7
text: I am … (2 x 2 attention matrix)

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_8
text: I am going … (3 x 3 attention matrix)

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_9
text: I am going to … (4 x 4 attention matrix)

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_10
AI engineering_KV Cache_11
text: This becomes very slow for long texts.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_12
text: KV caching reuses previous computations by storing them in memory. Instead of redoing the full attention calculation every time, the model stores the cell values (from attention) for past tokens.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_13
text: When it generates the next word, it only needs to calculate the query for that word, and reuse the previously saved cell values.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_14
text: This speeds things up massively. Most production-grade LLMs (like GPT-4, LLaMA, Mistral, etc.) use KV caching

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_15
text: Autoregressive transformers slow down as sequence length grows because each new token must attend over all previous tokens. Without optimization, this makes inference **quadratic** in sequence length.

id: AI engineering_KV Cache_16
text: **KV caching** solves this by storing Key (K) and Value (V) vectors for past tokens so they do not need to be recomputed. This reduces compute from **O(n²) → O(n)**.

id: AI engineering_Why Transformer Inference Is Slow_0
text: During generation at step *t*, naïve decoding recomputes:

id: AI engineering_Why Transformer Inference Is Slow_1
text: - hidden states - all Keys - all Values

id: AI engineering_Why Transformer Inference Is Slow_2
text: for every token up to *t-1*.

id: AI engineering_Complexity_0
text: - Work per token ≈ *(n × L × H)* - Total inference cost ≈ **O(n²)**

id: AI engineering_KV Caching: Core Idea_0
text: Compute **K** and **V** once per token, store them, and reuse later.

id: AI engineering_Mathematical Form_0
text: For token i:

id: AI engineering_Mathematical Form_1
text: Attention now becomes: $$ \text{Attn}(Q_t, K_{\text{cache}}, V_{\text{cache}}) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_t\, K_{\text{cache}}^{\mathsf{T}}}{\sqrt{d}}\right) \, V_{\text{cache}} $$

id: AI engineering_Code_0
text: > **Example: “I love cats”**

id: AI engineering_Without caching_0
text: - For “love”: recompute K/V for “I” - For “cats”: recompute K/V for “I”, “love”

id: AI engineering_With caching_0
text: - Compute K/V for “I” once - Reuse for all later tokens

id: AI engineering_Key Takeaways_0
text: - Naïve decoding → **O(n²)** - KV caching → **O(n)** - Cache grows linearly → memory becomes the bottleneck - All modern inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT‑LLM, HF Transformers) rely heavily on KV caching (KVCACHE: /assets/images/ai/kvCACHE.png)

id: AI engineering_Key Takeaways_1
text: For each transformer layer and each attention head, the model maintains separate KV caches. When generating the nth token, the cache stores K and V matrices for all n-1 previous tokens.

id: AI engineering_Key Takeaways_2
text: Obviously as we are storing such huge matrices in cache -> we need memory but that's okay, it's a tradeoff between computing them real time vs having memory. Computation trumps Memory when it comes to GPUs. (beautiful blog on this: https://medium.com/@prathamgrover777/kv-caching-attention-optimization-from-o-n%C2%B2-to-o-n-8b605f0d4072)

id: AI engineering_Key Takeaways_3
text: > programming section

id: AI engineering_Key Takeaways_4
text: **Q. KV Cache Code in PyTorch**

id: AI engineering_Key Takeaways_5
text: > **Common Mistake:** Not clearing KV cache between different conversations causes context contamination. The cache stores ALL previous tokens, so a new query will see tokens from previous conversations, leading to irrelevant information in responses and potential privacy issues. Always clear the cache between users or conversations.

id: AI engineering_Some GPU Terms_0
text: - SRAM (Static Random Access Memory) - DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory)

id: AI engineering_Some GPU Terms_1
text: In the context of GPUs utilizing SRAM, the "static" in SRAM indicates that it does not require refresh cycles, making it suitable for fast access and minimizing latency. Conversely, "dynamic" in DRAM implies that it needs regular refreshing to maintain the stored data, which can contribute to longer access times

id: AI engineering_Some GPU Terms_2
text: Great place to learn (GPU terms: https://modal.com/gpu-glossary)

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_0
text: **Problem:**

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_1
text: - Attention computes large matrices (QKᵀ , softmax, etc.). - Consumes a lot of memory and has poor hardware efficiency.

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_2
text: **Solution:**

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_3
text: - Flash Attention fuses softmax + matmul into one GPU kernel. - Uses tiling and streaming — loads only small parts of Q, K, V into GPU memory at a time. - Reduces total reads and writes. - Enables faster attention with lower peak memory.

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_4
text: Fundamentally LLM uses GPU, tons of parallel instructions, and own memory space (Static RAM) which loads memory from DRAM. This loading is an IO call and is slow.

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_5
text: So loading data from DRAM -> SRAM everytime you perform matrix mul is slow.

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_6
text: - Perform all operations together, get result for a particular Attention Block. - Each block attention is computed -> results are all aggregated and put together.

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_7
text: *Benefits*

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_8
text: - 10-20x lower memory consumption - 2-4x speedup! - You can perform flash attention along KV Caching and PagedAttention (later)

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_9
text: **Fundamentally**

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_10
text: GPU spends time doing 2 things -> computing matrices {matrix * matrix} & loading data from memory for previous tokens {matrix * vector}

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_11
text: Attention formulas revisited:

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_12
text: $$ S = \frac{QK^{\mathsf{T}}}{\text{scaling_factor}} $$

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_13
text: $$ \text{attention} = \mathrm{softmax}(S) $$

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_14
text: $$ \text{output} = \text{attention} \cdot V $$

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_15
text: Let's just take the main matrix multiplication operation: Q * K.T

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_16
text: **How does this happen on a GPU and why do we need flash attention at all?**

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_17
text: > gpu time

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_18
text: This operation happens on the HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) outside the GPU cores

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_19
text: - Load Q, K by blocks from HBM -> Compute dot product -> Save result S back to HBM - Load S from HBM -> Compute attention -> Save results A (attention) back to HBM - Load A, V from HBM -> Compute output matrix -> Save results O back to HBM

id: AI engineering_Flash Attention Quick Review_20
text: This back and forth travelling from HBM -> GPU Cores back to -> HBM **takes a lot of time!!**

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_0
text: Memory revision (keep this in mind)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_1
text: - CPU has DRAM (>1TB ) - GPU has HBM on the outside (40gb) - GPU on_chip has SRAM (20mb)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_2
text: Goal is to shift these matrices to *on_chip* and have it do calculation there itself instead of travelling back and forth. **Problem** is SRAM is only 20mb and we can't fit the entire attention matrix in it.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_3
text: > Enter Tiling

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_4
text: Matrix Multiplication Revisited: (Without Tiling: /assets/images/ai/without_tiling.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_5
text: For 4x4 matrix

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_6
text: - To compute each value we need to load 1 row value from vector A and 1 column value from vector B:: So total 8 memory accesses and in total (4 rows 4 columns) : 8*4 = 32 memory accesses.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_7
text: We need this number to go down.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_8
text: What if we do block multiplication of these matrices? Instead of individually calculating dot products (taking 1 row value and 1 column value) if we take 2x2 blocks of data and compute their matrix multiplication together we would have 8*2 = 16 memory accesses.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_9
text: So by calculating N*N blocks we reduce memory access by 1/N. **This is huge!!** (With Tiling: /assets/images/ai/withTiling.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_10
text: Partition the matrices A, B and C into 2x2 blocks.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_11
text: Now these 2x2 blocks can be moved to on_chip SRAM for faster processing and then combine these partial tile matrix multiplications to get final results. (SRAM Tiling: /assets/images/ai/tilingSRAM.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_12
text: How do you apply this to attention? We have already figured out the matrix multiplication part. What about the softmax part? $$ \mathrm{softmax}(x_i) = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{x_j}} $$

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_13
text: where xi are the features of the model.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_14
text: Let's take 1 row of the attention matrix. (Softmax: /assets/images/ai/softmax.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_15
text: To fix the overflow we use a little trick of subtracting m (the max val of sequence from each input (prevents overflow issue now all values are <= 0)) :: This is known as *Safe Softmax.* (Safe Softmax: /assets/images/ai/safesoftmax.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_16
text: - Find max - Caclulate sum of all e^x - Normalise by subtracting m

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_17
text: This process is IO intensive -> iterating the sequennce 3 times, how do we reduce this?

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_18
text: We can combine first and second pass by removing subtracting m in the second pass itself.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_19
text: We find a recurrence relation (again you must have heard this in your algorithms class) and then make the 3 step process -> 2 step (Recurrence Relation 3->2: /assets/images/ai/3-twostepsoftsoftmax.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_20
text: Apply same idea to self attention. $$ x_i = q\,k^{\mathsf{T}} $$

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_21
text: xi are the pre-softmax logits computed by dot product, we can use the same technique (instead of 3 passes -> 2 passes)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_22
text: Applying the same trick again we can reduce 2 passes -> 1 pass hence only 1 access to the memory for softmax. (FlashAttention: /assets/images/ai/flashAttention.png)

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_23
text: *Figure 4.1: Flash Attention algorithm showing tiling strategy and kernel fusion - reduces memory bandwidth by 2-4x through on-chip SRAM computation.*

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_24
text: Flash Attention fuses all computations together, and we still get same results.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_25
text: **Recap:**

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_26
text: - Partition Matrix (Q,K,V) into tiles. First Q,K,V vectors go to HBM -> onchip SRAM and we perform attention and get o1 (partial result saved to HBM) - Load next tile, perform attention in SRAM and update partial results from o1 -> o1' - Repeat this for all tiles - End of Loop we have all attention results for Q1, similarily we do this for Q2 and all further query vectors.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_27
text: There are even further optimisations to this like FlashAttention2 and FlashAttention3 Paper, but that is out of scope for this blog.

id: AI engineering_Speeding this up_28
text: I know this explanation wasn't enough so here is -

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_0
text: "Tiling" which is used to reduce global memory accesses by taking advantage of the shared memory on the GPU. Tiling can be seen as a way to boost execution efficiency of the kernel

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_1
text: Since everything is matrix multiplication, we better make sure it's as optimised as it can be.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_2
text: Some basic CUDA terms (CUDA is the software where matrix multiplication and all model compute happens, developed by Nvidia, it is low-level platform for accelerated computing, it is the same as low level memory) you should know if you have taken an OS class.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_3
text: - Thread: single unit of execution (each thread has its own memory called registers) - Block: group of threads (think process) : all threads in a block has access to shared memory. - Grid: group of blocks (access to global memory and constant memory)

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_4
text: *Input*: Two 4x4 matrices A, B.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_5
text: *Output*: 4x4 matrix C.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_6
text: C consists of 16 elements, where each element is computed through a dot product of a row of A and a column of B, then let's launch 16 threads, where each thread calculates 1 output element

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_7
text: Threads can be organised into 2x2 block hence 4 blocks in a grid.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_8
text: What does each thread do? Responsible for loading input elements into shared memory (within each block) :: Hence each of the 4 threads in this block can see what other three threads do. {mini-matrix multiplcation using shared memory} :: storing temp result and then continue summing the temp results of next mini-matrix multiplication.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_9
text: When we are finished with each individual mini-matrix multiplication, each thread would load their corresponding result to the output C element that they are mapped to.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_10
text: **Without tiling:** In order to calculate one output element, a thread will need to access one entire row of input A and one entire column of input B, for calculating the dot product. In our example, that is 8 accesses per thread.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_11
text: **With tiling:** Each thread ends up loading two elements from input A and two elements from input B, which totals up to 4 accesses per thread.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_12
text: Let’s say we multiply two large square matrices of size S×S, where S is a multiple of 32. Obviously, the result is also a square matrix of size S×S.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_13
text: With naïve algorithm, to compute each element of the result, we gonna need to fetch S elements from both matrices. The output matrix has $S^2$ elements, therefore the total count of loaded elements is $$2*S^3$$

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_14
text: With 32×32 tiling, to compute each 32×32 tile of the result, we gonna need to fetch S/32 tiles from both matrices.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_15
text: The output size in tiles is $(S/32)^2$, the total count of loaded tiles is $$2*(S/32)^3$$ Each 32×32 tile contains $$32^2$$ elements, the total count of loaded elements is therefore $$(32^2)*2*(S/32)^3 = (2/32)*S^3$$

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_16
text: Hence the tiling reduced global memory bandwidth by the factor of 32, which is a huge performance win.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_17
text: Since every layer has to compute matrix multiplication again and again, we must make it faster::

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_18
text: Efficient matrix multiplication employs a tiling strategy. The large matrix operation gets divided into smaller tiles that fit in shared memory, reducing expensive global memory accesses.

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_19
text: > programming section

id: AI engineering_More on Tiling (read this slowly)_20
text: **Q. Flash Attention**

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_0
text: **Problem**

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_1
text: Predicting how big KV cache memory will be is difficult - the next token could be one word, one sentence, or one paragraph. Transformers can't tell how large the answer is going to be, so we don't know how large the KV Cache memory needs to be.

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_2
text: In production we have limited memory, if we don't know how big our context length is -> we can overallocate KV Cache (memory intensive) or underallocate (small KV -> recompute) :: *BIG ISSUE*

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_3
text: 40-60% memory is wasted due to this.

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_4
text: Improvement: Paged attention (if you took an OS class, this will sound familiar!) = Dynamic size of cache for each request (100% utilization) {No cache misses}

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_5
text: Cache -> Virtual Blocks -> Physical Blocks (not contigious) {Exactly how (paging: https://www.scaler.com/topics/paging-in-os/)

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_6
text: works in OS} (Pagin2: /assets/images/ai/paging2.png) (Paging: /assets/images/ai/paging.png)

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_7
text: In transformers, KV caching stores token-to-token attention scores in an N x N matrix.

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_8
text: We don't know how large the output will be, so guessing the final number N is impossible. This means we can’t allocate the exact fixed memory to the matrix (N x N).

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_9
text: Instead we choose a large safe value of N like 2000, resulting in a massive 2000 x 2000 matrix space allocation for a single attention process.

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_10
text: This leads to fragmentation and wasted memory, especially in real-time systems. Solution:

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_11
text: - Use fixed-size memory pages instead of trying to allocate the entire buffer up front. - Each page stores part of the KV cache. If the output is longer, just add more pages.

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_12
text: > Paged Attention an attention algorithm inspired by the classic idea of virtual memory and paging in operating systems. Unlike the traditional attention algorithms, PagedAttention allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space. Specifically, PagedAttention partitions the KV cache of each sequence into blocks, each block containing the keys and values for a fixed number of tokens. During the attention computation, the PagedAttention kernel identifies and fetches these blocks efficiently. (Page Attention: /assets/images/ai/pageAttention1.png)

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_13
text: Because the blocks do not need to be contiguous in memory, we can manage the keys and values in a more flexible way as in OS’s virtual memory: one can think of blocks as pages, tokens as bytes, and sequences as processes.

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_14
text: Page attention also does efficient memory sharing so multiple output sequences are generated from same prompt, this helps in chain of thought and computation and memory for prompt is shared (just how processes share physical pages in OS) (Parallel Page Attention: /assets/images/ai/parallelPageAttention.png) (beautiful blog on this: https://blog.vllm.ai/2023/06/20/vllm.html)

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_15
text: Advantage of this (Reasoning):

id: AI engineering_Paged Attention: Efficient Memory Management_16
text: - Some words are same, attention block can be stored in phyiscal memory and can be shared among multiple processes. 1 phyiscal attention blog -> many virutual attention blog each comes with different branches springing from original prefix and model can pick the best branch. (Reasoning Page: /assets/images/ai/reasoning_paging.png)

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_0
text: The idea is to activate only a small part of the model for any given input.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_1
text: You treat the neural network as a graph and activate a subgraph based on the input query.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_2
text: - For example, a query about shopping might trigger a different part of the model than a query about emotions. - Only a few "experts" or parts of the model are active at any time.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_3
text: This reduces compute cost while still leveraging a very large overall model.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_4
text: The takeaway is that MoE improves efficiency by routing inputs through specialized parts of the model rather than using the full network for every request.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_5
text: Activate subgraphs which are expert in those queries (Kind of like load balancer)

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_6
text: *Advantage*: Number of neurons that are going to be fired are less but capbility is same as LLM

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_7
text: Gate chooses top1/top2 subgraph which has the answer. (More on this: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668) (MOE: /assets/images/ai/moe.png) (MOE_Correct: /assets/images/ai/moe_correct.png) (MOE_Wrong: /assets/images/ai/moe_wrong.png) (LB MOE: /assets/images/ai/lb_MOE.png)

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_8
text: The router decides which expert sub-model to choose for a query typically during the inference phase rather than the training phase.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_9
text: During training, the model might use a labeled dataset to learn how to associate specific queries with the appropriate sub-models, often employing techniques such as routing algorithms to optimize for query handling

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_10
text: **Problem:**

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_11
text: - Scaling LLMs with more parameters = more compute. - But you don’t always need the full model for every input. A small section of the LLM would suffice, depending on the input query.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_12
text: **Solution:**

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_13
text: - Split the model into experts (independent subnetworks). - Use a gating mechanism to activate only a few experts per input. - Reduces compute but keeps the model expressive.

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_14
text: **Example**:

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_15
text: - Input 1: “Translate to French” → Activates Experts 2 and 4 - Input 2: “Summarize this text” → Activates Experts 1 and 5

id: AI engineering_MOE (Mixture of experts)_16
text: Each forward pass uses only ~10% of the total parameters.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_0
text: **1. Quantisation** : Converting higher bits -> lower bits of model floating points numbers without losing much precision and accuracy.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_1
text: > Taking weights of model and representing them using fewer bits.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_2
text: The cache in KV Cache grows linearly with sequence length. For a 13-billion parameter model like LLaMA-2, each output token requires approximately 1 MB of cache storage.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_3
text: A 4,000 token context needs about 4 GB just for the cache, comparable to the model size itself.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_4
text: Way to improve this is to quantise (FP16 -> FP8 : basically lowering the amount of bits you use to store vectors without losing precision / accuracy) or using sliding window attention that only retains recent tokens or implementing attention approximations that reduce cache requirements.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_5
text: A 7-billion parameter model at FP16 precision requires approximately 14 GB of memory (7B parameters × 2 bytes per parameter). Quantizing to INT4 reduces this to 3.5 GB, enabling inference on consumer hardware. (beautiful blog on quantisation: https://medium.com/@prathamgrover777/intro-to-quantization-in-llms-adfae03bf447)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_6
text: **Q. Perform Quantisation on vanilla model.pt -> Convert to FP16 (32 bits -> 16 bits)**

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_7
text: Trained model -> .pt

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_8
text: - First convert it to .onnx (platform independent model file)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_9
text: Then convert to TensorRT (model.plan) using trtexec engine or python script below:

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_10
text: Now your model goes from .pt -> FP16 .plan which is *significanty faster* at inference/prediction time.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_11
text: Typical results (RTX 3090 / A100 class GPUs):

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_12
text: - **ResNet-50:** 4× faster - **YOLOv5/YOLOv8 Object Detection:** 2.5–3× faster - **Transformers:** 2–3× faster

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_13
text: Memory depends on : total weights, how deep those connections are (how many bits are required to store weights)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_14
text: - Since weights are smaller, you can store more weights in cache -> faster inference.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_15
text: **When to perform quantisation?**

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_16
text: - Step1: Train LLM - Step2: Answer queries (You perform the quantisation part here)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_17
text: **2. Sparse Attention**

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_18
text: Take one token and only focus on those queries that are near it.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_19
text: **Idea:** relevant context for a token lies near the token itself, we don't have to search the entire space. (Sparse Attention: /assets/images/ai/sparseAttn.png)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_20
text: For damaged we only need to look at the damaged column for relevant context.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_21
text: **Example**

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_22
text: In Harry Potter novel, if he's angry, hes angry recently (context) not 5 pages ago (and its being addressed now (highly improbable)) (HP Sparse: /assets/images/ai/harryPottersparse.png)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_23
text: Attention is only computed for these (diagonal) cells in the matrix

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_24
text: This significantly reduces computed : O(n*n) -> O(n*w) where w is the diagonal length

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_25
text: - Drawback context window is shorter (if from 3 pages ago it wont' pick that up) *{but its a tradeoff}*

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_26
text: - If input is only a sentence -> dense / normal attention - If input is an entire document (harry potter book) -> sparse attention (Sparse Diagonal: /assets/images/ai/diagonalSparse.png) (Dense vs Sparse: /assets/images/ai/denseVsSparse.png)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_27
text: *Smarter way to do this* (Google Big Bard: /assets/images/ai/local_global_sparse.png)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_28
text: - Drawback Tradeoff between accuracy and speed - Flash Attention is computed using GPUs, in sparse attn -> you have this thick diagonal but how do you send it to the GPU. - Look these random cells -> GPU doesn't get a complete block it only gets cells, then flash attention doesn't work because that only works in blocks (FA) - So you can have random blocks for sparse attention and local attention can be found and then entire block can be sent to GPUs for flash attention to work. - But this is harder to implement and not widely used. - GPU centric optimisations is hard (deepseek has made it work) - SLM and Distillation

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_29
text: **3. Q. Distillation (Optimizations used in deployment)**

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_30
text: - Reduce number of parameters (weights) in model. - Reduce parameters in FFN : smaller model which also works well (Small Language Model) 100 Billion parametrer -> 100 million parameter (lossy (less intelligent) but covers most use cases as long as you fine tune the model.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_31
text: This is called distillation.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_32
text: > Large language model: Teacher, student is the smaller language model.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_33
text: Same input for both model, see output for both and compare outputs (difference & backpropagation fixes it) (Distillation: /assets/images/ai/distillation.png)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_34
text: Student tries to mimics teachers (kind of like (GANs: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_35
AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_36
text: - Drawback: reduced intelligence. - Speculative Decoding

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_37
text: LLMs generate one token at a time. This creates latency, especially for long answers.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_38
text: Speculative Decoding uses a smaller model to speculate on the next few tokens. The large model verifies or corrects them in parallel.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_39
text: Process:

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_40
text: - Small model predicts the next 4–8 tokens. - Large model checks these predictions. - If valid, the LLM accepts; else correct this token and send to SLM for further processing.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_41
text: **Example:** “What is 319 ÷ 215?”

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_42
text: Small model predicts: “The result is 2.59.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_43
text: Large model verifies all tokens in parallel (green / red are predictions).

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_44
text: - Verification 1 -- <empty> (The) - Verification 2 -- The- (result) - Verification 3 -- The result- (is) - Verification 4 -- The result is- (1.48)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_45
text: It finds the token "2.59" incorrect, and replaces it with "1.48"

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_46
text: Large model now asks Small model to predict the rest of the sequence.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_47
text: This happens recursively until full output is generated.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_48
text: This results in **2x** faster decoding without accuracy loss.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_49
text: *Different tokens require different efforts*

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_50
text: - Query : what is 5+2 - Output: the answer to 5+2 is 7 (most effort required was at 7, rest were easy)

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_51
text: This works because gpt is trained on facts so if it has seen 5+2 many times on the internet the next token is probably 7 and hence it guesses that, it doesn't mathematiclaly computer or anything, it is only trained on data.

id: AI engineering_Optimisation Techniques with Tradeoffs_52
text: Corrections required are done by LLM, rest is done by small language model, basically teacher who checks output of student in every token. **simple yet brilliant concept.** (Speculation1: /assets/images/ai/different_efforts.png) (Speculation2: /assets/images/ai/speculation2.png) (Speculation3: /assets/images/ai/Speculation.png)

id: AI engineering_Optimization Techniques Comparison_0
text: | Technique | Speedup | Memory Impact | Quality Loss | |-----------|---------|---------------|--------------| | **KV Cache** | 3-5x | +80% (cache growth) | None | | **Flash Attention** | 2-4x | -50% (peak usage) | None | | **Quantization (INT8)** | 2-3x | -75% | <1% accuracy loss | | **Quantization (INT4)** | 3-4x | -87% | 2-3% accuracy loss | | **Paged Attention** | 1.2-1.5x | +20% utilization | None | | **Sparse Attention** | 2-10x | -60% | 2-5% accuracy loss | | **Speculative Decoding** | 2-3x | +30% (dual models) | None | | **Distillation (SLM)** | 5-10x | -90% | 10-20% capability loss | | **MOE** | 2-4x | 0% (sparse activation) | None |

id: AI engineering_Optimization Techniques Comparison_1
text: > **Key Concept:** Optimizations compound! Combining KV cache (3x) + Flash attention (2x) + INT8 (2x) = ~12x total speedup. Don't optimize in isolation - apply multiple techniques together for maximum impact.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_0
text: We've covered the optimization techniques that make production LLMs practical. These aren't optional - they're essential for real-world deployment:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_1
text: **Core Optimizations:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_2
text: - **KV caching**: Store computed attention keys/values to avoid recomputation (O(n²) → O(n)) - **Flash attention**: Fuse operations and use tiling to minimize memory bandwidth (2-4x speedup, 10-20x less memory) - **Quantization**: Reduce precision (FP32 → INT8/INT4) for 4x+ speedup with minimal accuracy loss - **Paged attention**: Manage variable-length sequences efficiently using virtual memory concepts - **Sparse attention**: Only compute attention for nearby tokens (reduces O(n²) to O(n×w)) - **Speculative decoding**: Use small model to predict, large model to verify (2-3x faster)

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_3
text: **Trade-offs to Consider:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_4
text: - **Memory vs Speed**: KV cache uses more memory but enables faster generation - **Accuracy vs Efficiency**: Quantization and sparse attention sacrifice some quality for significant speedup - **Complexity vs Gains**: Advanced techniques (MOE, sparse attention) add implementation complexity

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_5
text: **Why This Matters:** Without these optimizations:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_6
text: - A single chatbot response could take minutes instead of seconds - You'd need 10x more GPUs to serve the same number of users - Costs would be prohibitively high for most applications

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_7
text: **Production Reality:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_8
text: - vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and other inference engines combine these techniques - Real systems use KV cache + flash attention + quantization together - Memory bandwidth (not compute) is often the bottleneck

id: AI engineering_Chapter 5: Key Takeaways_9
text: **Next Steps:** Now that we understand how LLMs work and how to make them fast, we need to make them **useful**. Chapter 6 covers production patterns: RAG for grounding responses in facts, AI agents for tool use, and cost optimization strategies for real applications.

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: RAG, AI Agents & Production Deployment_1
text: Understanding LLMs is one thing. Deploying them to solve real problems is another. This chapter covers the application layer - the patterns and techniques that make LLMs useful beyond just "complete this text":

metadata.section: Chapter 6: RAG, AI Agents & Production Deployment

metadata.section: Chapter 6: RAG, AI Agents & Production Deployment

id: AI engineering_RAG_0
text: Information not necessarily in weights but you give it external relevant sources of data. In this way it is able to AUGMENT the knowledge base of LLM with relevant documents. (RAG WITH CLI: /assets/images/ai/rag_with_cli.png)

id: AI engineering_RAG_1
text: So every LLM learns in 3 ways:

id: AI engineering_RAG_2
text: - Model pre training (data + gpu) - Model fine tuning (gpu + data)

id: AI engineering_RAG_3
text: - Passing contextual info (data)

id: AI engineering_RAG_4

id: AI engineering_RAG_5
text: Imagine chatGPT with your custom notes for OS. How easy would it be to study for the exam.

id: AI engineering_RAG_6
text: The model can answer all queries using your notes. Why is this so benefital? Instead of giving it a very big sample space of data to search for, we limit it (reducing $$ and GPU compute required)

id: AI engineering_RAG_7
text: This is benefitial for small companies that want to build a customer support chatbot which accesses all company relevant documents and only answers using them (eg: Zomato, MMT) instead of building a LLM from scratch which gives vague and general answers instead of niche company answers.

id: AI engineering_RAG_8
text: So you can have a personalised chatbot at the fraction of the cost of fine tuning.

id: AI engineering_RAG_9
text: So how does RAG work? Let's say you give it a prompt "My order #3129 wasn't delivered but shows out for delivery, can you help me with this" on Zomato, let's see how the flow goes::

id: AI engineering_RAG_10
text: - Index + Embedding - Since data is huge and cant pass everything in model prompt (> context length) so only give it relevant data. - Vector Store DB - Data is stored in chunks (which are converted to embeddings (words which are numbers) - Chunking happens by sentence or paragraph (there are multiple ways of doing this but just assume fixed size chunking for now (chunk of 100 words each)) - Contextual information about the document/external database is stored in vectors. Vector databases are designed for efficient storage of vectors which facilitates query interface that can retrieve at higher search rates and speeds.

id: AI engineering_RAG_11
text: . By controlling the chunk size, RAG can maintain a balance between comprehensiveness and precision. - Filtering + Ranking - Improving data quality :: Filtering - Content based filtering: filter out doc that don't contain 'xyz' - Metadata filtering : filter out doc based on author, source link etc. - Threshold filter: after initial retrieval, docu are filtered on basis of threshold similarity socre - Re-rank is used to order filtered doc to priortise those are relevant. - Semmantic Re-ranking:reorder based on semantic content (emotion) - Contextual re-ranking: reorder based on contextual info - LTR (learning to rank) : ML model used (LambdaNet) trained to predict relevant of documents (features: doc length, chat history, term frequency) - Retrieval - Searching can be via KNN, ANN, Tree Based ( (Annoy: https://github.com/spotify/annoy)

id: AI engineering_RAG_12
text: ), Clustering (FAISS) etc.. - Prompt Augmentation - Ingestion of retrived doc in prompt of model so model can generate response - Generation - Personalised + high quality result according to user need by comvining existing knowledge + relevant data in prompt

id: AI engineering_RAG_13
text: Graph databases are preferred over vector databases (they allow for semantically similar vector searches but way fetch irrelevant data) :: Graph extracts entity-relationship data but it also requires exact query matching (no semantic similarity) so both have their tradeoffs.

id: AI engineering_RAG_14
text: After retrieving -> filter by adding ranking and only keep top-k results. (RAG PIPELINE: /assets/images/ai/rag_pipeline.png) (Sentence Window: /assets/images/ai/sentence-window-retrieval.png)

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_0
text: Even with RAG, LLMs can still hallucinate or provide inaccurate information. Here are strategies to improve quality:

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_1
text: **1. Ground prompts with facts**

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_2
text: - Use RAG to feed real documents into context - Provide specific, relevant sources rather than generic context

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_3
text: **2. Reduce prompt scope**

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_4
text: - Don't stuff 20 documents into every query - Smaller, targeted context = sharper, more accurate responses - Use semantic search to find the MOST relevant chunks

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_5
text: **3. Force answer shape**

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_6
text: - Add explicit instructions: "Answer ONLY based on documents provided" - "If information is not in the context, say 'I don't have enough information'" - Constrain the model's behavior through prompts

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_7
text: **4. Validation and post-processing**

id: AI engineering_Reducing Hallucinations with RAG_8
text: - Apply business rules: "If model says '7 days', verify against actual policy" - Use confidence scores to flag uncertain responses - Human-in-the-loop for critical decisions

id: AI engineering_Prompt Engineering: Getting Better Outputs_0
text: One of the most practical skills for working with LLMs is **prompt engineering** - the art of crafting inputs to get better outputs.

id: AI engineering_Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Prompting_0
text: **Zero-Shot:** Give the model a task with no examples

id: AI engineering_Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Prompting_1
text: **Few-Shot:** Provide examples to guide the response format

id: AI engineering_Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Prompting_2
text: Few-shot prompting is almost always better - the model picks up on the format and style from your examples.

id: AI engineering_Chain of Thought in Prompts_0

id: AI engineering_Chain of Thought in Prompts_1

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_0
text: **The Problem:** System prompts alone have limitations:

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_1
text: - Can't contain all relevant information (token limits) - Lack real-time data - Missing user-specific context

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_2
text: **The Solution:** Combine multiple sources:

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_3
text: **Context Engineering:** As chat history grows, you can't pass everything to the LLM (memory limits). Strategies:

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_4
text: - **Summarization:** Compress chat history into key points - **Sliding window:** Keep only recent N messages - **Importance filtering:** Extract most relevant information

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_5
text: This ensures the model has context without hitting token limits.

id: AI engineering_System Prompts + Context Engineering_6

id: AI engineering_Cost Optimization Strategies_0
text: Running LLMs in production can get expensive. Here are strategies to reduce costs:

id: AI engineering_1. Caching_0
text: - **Vector-based caching:** Common queries ("What's the weather?") get cached responses - Store query vectors, return cached answers for similar queries - Works like a hashmap: Key = Query Vector, Value = Response

id: AI engineering_2. Model Selection_0
text: - Use smaller models when appropriate (Mistral, DeepSeek instead of GPT-4) - Reserve expensive models for complex tasks

id: AI engineering_3. Token Reduction_0
text: - Reduce context window size - Compress system prompts - Limit chat history

id: AI engineering_4. Rate Limiting_0
text: - Per-user query limits - Per-session throttling

id: AI engineering_5. AI Agents for Better UX_0

id: AI engineering_5. AI Agents for Better UX_1
text: AI agents can understand intent and provide better answers using context (user's previous purchases, size history) without multiple back-and-forth queries - saving tokens and improving experience.

id: AI engineering_6. Security & Privacy_0
text: - **Anonymize queries:** Don't store personally identifiable information - **Filter sensitive data:** Remove credit card numbers, emails before logging - **Data retention policies:** Delete query logs after N days

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_0
text: We've explored how to deploy LLMs in production and make them solve real-world problems:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_1
text: **Core Patterns:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_2
text: - **RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)**: Ground LLM outputs in retrieved documents to reduce hallucinations and add up-to-date information - **AI Agents**: Enable LLMs to use tools (search, calculators, code execution, APIs) to handle tasks they can't solve through text generation alone - **Vector search in RAG**: Chunk documents → embed → store in vector DB → retrieve similar chunks for context - **Tool calling**: LLMs learn during fine-tuning when to call external tools instead of generating text

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_3
text: **Production Considerations:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_4
text: - **Cost optimization strategies**: - Vector-based caching for common queries - Choose smaller models (Mistral, DeepSeek) when appropriate - Reduce token counts through prompt optimization - Rate limiting per user/session - **Quality improvements**: - Ground prompts with facts (RAG) - Reduce prompt scope (targeted context, not entire knowledge base) - Force answer structure ("Answer only from provided documents") - Post-processing validation rules

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_5
text: **Why This Matters:** Raw LLMs are powerful but not production-ready. They:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_6
text: - Hallucinate confidently - Can't access real-time data - Can't perform precise computations - Lack domain-specific knowledge

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_7
text: RAG and agents solve these problems by combining LLM reasoning with:

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_8
text: - Retrieved factual documents (RAG) - External tools and APIs (agents) - Structured validation (prompt engineering)

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_9
text: **The Complete Stack:**

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_10
text: 1. **Foundation**: Vector embeddings (Ch 1) + Vector DBs (Ch 2) 2. **Preprocessing**: Tokenization (Ch 3) 3. **Model**: Transformers (Ch 4) 4. **Optimization**: KV cache, flash attention, quantization (Ch 5) 5. **Application**: RAG + AI agents (Ch 6)

id: AI engineering_Chapter 6: Key Takeaways_11
text: You now have a complete understanding of the AI engineering stack - from mathematical foundations to production deployment. The conclusion provides final thoughts and resources for going deeper.

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_0
text: **The Foundation (Chapters 1-2):**

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_1
text: - Vector embeddings compress complex objects into fixed-dimensional spaces - Similarity in vector space corresponds to semantic similarity - Vector databases (pgVector, Milvus) provide specialized storage and sub-linear search through HNSW, IVF, and other ANN algorithms - **Vector Embeddings:** Vector embeddings compress complex objects into fixed-dimensional spaces where semantic similarity equals spatial proximity, enabling efficient similarity search through distance calculations. - Specialized vector databases use ANN algorithms (HNSW, IVF) and compression techniques (Product Quantization, Scalar Quantization) to enable sub-linear search across billion-vector datasets.

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_2
text: **The Preprocessing (Chapter 3):**

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_3
text: - Tokenization bridges human language and neural networks - BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) strikes the optimal balance between vocabulary size and meaning preservation - Every LLM interaction starts with text → tokens → embeddings

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_4
text: **The Model (Chapter 4):**

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_5
text: - Transformers use self-attention to let every token attend to every other token - Multi-head attention captures different types of relationships (syntax, semantics, dependencies) - Stacking 96+ layers builds progressively abstract representations - Positional encodings and causal masking are crucial architectural details - Transformers use multi-head self-attention across 96+ stacked layers to understand context, then undergo pre-training → (SFT: https://cameronrwolfe.substack.com/p/understanding-and-using-supervised)

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_6
text: → (RLHF: https://www.superannotate.com/blog/rlhf-for-llm)

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_7
text: to become instruction-following assistants like ChatGPT.

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_8
text: **The Optimization (Chapter 5):**

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_9
text: - KV caching reduces inference from O(n²) to O(n) - Flash attention minimizes memory bandwidth through tiling - Quantization enables 4x+ speedups with minimal quality loss - Production systems combine these techniques for practical deployment

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_10
text: **The Application (Chapter 6):**

id: AI engineering_The Complete Pipeline_11
text: - RAG grounds LLMs in retrieved documents to reduce hallucinations - AI agents give LLMs access to tools for tasks they can't solve through text alone - Cost optimization and prompt engineering make systems economically viable (Complete AI Engineering Pipeline: /assets/images/ai/pipeline.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_0
text: > introduced in DeepSeek-v2 paper, fraction of resources + outperforms standard MHA

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_1
text: - We all know Mult-Head attention works, but it has a huge problem -> KV cache is HUGEEE. How do we reduce this space? - This is how attention scores look like for a normal MHA - ! (attention_scores: /assets/images/paper/attention_mha.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_2
text: - *i* = i-th attention head, *j* = indexes over all previous tokens in sequence (from 1 -> t) - *dh* = dimension of each attention head = ( total embedding dimension of model ) / number_of_heads - *softmax* = attention score (converts logits to [0-1] probability ensuring they sum to 1) ~ normalisation - outputs from all attention heads are concatenated to a single vector * Weight matrix $W_o$ - Converts back to original embedded dimension (so that attention input = output dimension) - $K_t$ and $V_t$ are stored in a cache so when new token comes in, it doesn't have to calculate k, v for all previous tokens again to compute attention scores. Since we are only having new Q every time, K and V stay the same for previous tokens. *This is smart, but we do need to store this K and V for previous tokens somewhere right? We store it in a cache. KV-Cache 101.* - Storing KV Cache for every token = memory bottleneck - Don't just believe what you read, what do we mean by a memory bottleneck here? How to compute memory for this? - **start** - For each token: - [K1, K2, K3, .. K_number_of_heads] = number_of_heads * dimension_head for keys - [V1, V2, V3, .. V_number_of_heads] = number_of_heads * dimension_head for values - Total: 2 * number_of_heads * dimension_head - Sequence Length = L - Total Memory -> (2 * number_of_heads * dimension_heads * Length) - As Length grows -> 2 * number_of_heads * dimension_heads per token becomes LARGEEE. - **fin**

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_3
text: - Suffers from high KV-Cache requirements (inference bottleneck) - So how does MLA solve this? *drumroll*: compress key-value pairs. How though? *Low Rank Key-Value Joint Compression* - **Instead of storing full key-value pairs, MLA compresses them into a shared latent space and reconstruct K and V *only when needed***

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_4
text: - What are these Weight_down and Weight_up? **Projections** : Instead of storing K, V, store a small compressed vector.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_5
text: > Think of these projections like creating a detailed shadow of an object. The shadow is simpler and has fewer dimensions (it's 2D), but it still captures the object's essential shape. MLA creates a compressed 'shadow' of the Key and Value vectors, capturing the necessary information in a much smaller space."

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_6
text: - How to do this? Store weight_up_key, weight_up_val (Fixed weights of model, one-time storage cost) - MLA does have large projection matrices, they’re part of the model parameters (stored once) rather than per-token memory requirements. - Per-token memory (what we need to cache during inference) is just the small l-dimensional vector called compressed_kv - ! (cl: /assets/images/paper/commutative_law.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_7
text: - Only storing small compressed vectors for each token instead of full key-value pairs. Reduces KV Cache by **93.3%**

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_8
text: > one problem: ROPE is incompatible with low rank compression since ROPE = position sensitive to keys and queries making absorption impossible

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_9
text: RoPE is **position-sensitive** Low-rank compression is **linear algebra**

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_10
text: Traditional RoPE applies position encoding to both K and Q

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_11
text: This becomes problematic with compressed KV pairs because matrix multiplication isn’t commutative

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_12
text: So in MLA, we can’t merge RoPE with compressed representations efficiently

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_13
text: "The main issue is that RoPE is sensitive to the exact position of a token. The compression step in MLA, however, involves matrix multiplication which is not commutative (A B ≠ B A). This means you can't just apply RoPE before compression and expect it to work correctly afterward. The positional information gets scrambled.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_14
text: > To solve this, DeepSeek decouples it: they first create the compressed representations and then apply positional encodings to generate the final, position-aware keys and queries.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_15
text: - **Decouple positional and compressed components** - Apply RoPE *after* reconstruction

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_16
text: This is a classic example of: > A practical hack driven by math constraints

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_17
text: - Compressed query is projected to obtain the decoupled queries - Rope is then applied to this to obtain positional queries : result-> set of positional queries across all attention heads - Similarily, input tokens are projected to obtain decoupled keys, ROPE is applied to make these keys positional aware - These two vectors are concatenated (compressed repr and positional info) - Similarily this happens for Keys (not just Q) - Attention Score is calculated

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-Head Latent Attention_18
text: - ! (drope: /assets/images/paper/decoupledROPE.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_3
text: - Instead of one huge brain doing everything, MoE uses many small specialist brains, and a router that decides which ones to consult for each token.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_4
text: How standard transformer works (recap) Token → Attention → Feed-Forward Network (FFN) → Next layer

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_5

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_6

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_7

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_8
text: Instead of *1 FFN for all tokens* we get: *N experts (e.g. 256 FFNs)* from which only K experts are used per token (e.g. K = 2)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_9
text: > The expert selection process happens dynamically at each step of computation, where different experts can be activated even within the same sequence. The router network continuously evaluates which expert(s) should handle each part of the input or generation, making this a fine-grained, token-level division of labor rather than a coarse query-level split.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_28
text: **Q. What does the router do actually?** token_embedding → router → scores for each expert Then:

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_MOE_29

text: Important: Routing happens per token, not per sentence. (moe: /assets/images/paper/moe.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_0
text: MOE architecture consists of the following 2 components-

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_1
text: - Experts - Gating Network / Router

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_2
text: - Input Encoding - The input (token embedding) enters the model. - This embedding is sent both to the normal transformer path and to a gating (router) network. - The router’s job is only to decide which experts should handle this input.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_3
text: - Gating / Routing Decision - The gating network scores all available experts for the given input. - These scores represent how useful each expert would be for this input. - Usually, only the top-K experts (e.g. K=1 or 2) are selected.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_4
text: - Sparsity (Conditional Computation) - Instead of running all experts, the model runs only the selected ones. This is called sparse activation. - Result: - Massive model capacity - Low compute cost per token

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_5
text: - Expert Processing - Each selected expert is a small neural network (typically a Feed-Forward Network). - The same input is sent to each selected expert. - Each expert processes the input independently.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_6
text: - Expert Weighting - The output of each expert is scaled by its gating weight. - More relevant experts contribute more. - Less relevant experts contribute less.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_7
text: - Output Aggregation - The weighted outputs from the selected experts are combined (usually summed). - This combined output replaces the standard FFN output in the transformer layer.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_8
text: - Pass to Next Layer - The aggregated output is passed to the next transformer layer. - The process repeats for every MoE layer and every token

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_9
text: *tldr;*

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_10
text: - Router chooses experts - Only a few experts run - Outputs are weighted and combined - You get big-model intelligence at small-model cost (moe2: /assets/images/paper/moe2.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_11
text: Where can this be a problem? **Router collapse** (same expert always picked)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_12
text: - expert1: 5% - expert2': 2% - expert3': 1% - expert4: 6% - expert5: 76%

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_13
text: As you can see, this is not balanced at all. Workload isn't being distributed properly. If the same experts get picked:

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_14
text: - Others don’t train - Capacity is wasted - Performance drops

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_15
text: **Q. What is the problem?** Not only will there be an uneven distribution of experts chosen, but some experts will hardly be trained at all. This results in issues during both training and inference.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_16
text: Instead, we want equal importance among experts during training and inference. How to prevent overfitting on the same experts.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_17
text: **How to solve this? Load Balancing!!!!**

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_18
text: - DeepSeek v3 does Bias-Based Routing for DeepseekMoE - ! (bias: /assets/images/paper/bias.png)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_19
text: - score_for_routing = original_score + bias - For each expert after each training step: - If expert is overloaded: - bias -= γ (make them less likely to get picked next time) - If expert is underloaded: - bias += γ (make them more likely to get picked next time)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_20
text: > bias term (γ) is dynamically added or subtracted from an expert's score based on whether it is over- or under-loaded during training Maintains quality (original affinity scores) while achieving balance (through bias adjustments)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_21
text: > This is like a smart traffic controller at a busy intersection. If one road (expert) gets too congested, the controller adjusts the traffic lights (bias) to redirect cars (tokens) to less busy roads. The γ is like a small adjustment, ensuring the change isn't too drastic. This keeps traffic flowing smoothly without creating new jams elsewhere.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_22
text: Instead of adding a big auxiliary loss (which hurts quality), they:

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_23
text: - Add a **bias term** to routing scores - Adjust it dynamically based on expert load

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_24
text: This is subtle but important:

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_25
text: - Keeps routing *mostly semantic* - Gently nudges balance

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_26
text: When reading papers, look for: > “Does this fix introduce a new problem elsewhere?”

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_27
text: Here, the answer seems mostly **no**,

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Architecture of MOE_28

text: > Now let's look at the final optimisation DSv3 does:

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-token Prediction_0
text: - Most standard language models — like GPT, LLaMA, etc. — are trained with next-token prediction (NTP) - This is what people mean when they say the word *autoregressive* (one token at a time) - Multi-token prediction is basically predicting multiple future tokens at once (e.g., the next 𝑛 tokens) from the same input context - Instead of p(xt+1​ ∣ x1:t​), we do p(xt+1​, xt+2​, …, xt+n​∣x1:t​) - Each head predicts one future token. These predictions are trained jointly. - Training only: inference still generates one token at a time - Shared backbone: no extra transformer compute - Works best with long sequences

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-token Prediction_1
text: **Q. Why?**

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-token Prediction_2
text: - **Denser learning signal** - With next-token prediction, each training example yields one scalar loss. - With multi-token prediction, each position yields n prediction losses simultaneously. - More gradient signal per token (faster learning per example) - **Inference acceleration** - If you can predict multiple tokens in one pass, you reduce the number of sequential forward passes needed - Fewer sequential decoding step

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-token Prediction_3
text: **Q. How does this speed up inference?**

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-token Prediction_4
text: - A standard autoregressive model generates one token at a time, requiring one full forward pass of the model for each token. - To generate 100 tokens, it needs 100 sequential passes. - With MTP, if the model can predict, say, 3 tokens in a single pass, you might only need around 33 passes to generate the same 100 tokens. This reduction in the number of sequential steps is a major source of acceleration.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Multi-token Prediction_5
text: DeepseekV3 does the same, it doesn’t just train on next-token prediction. It also learns to predict several future tokens from each position, jointly, during training.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_How is it different than original MTP_0
text: - The original academic MTP proposal predicts all future tokens in parallel using independent heads at each position. - DeepSeek’s implementation is slightly different - From a single hidden state (hidden_state_t), the model uses multiple independent 'prediction heads.' Each head is trained to predict a different future token. - For example, head_1 predicts token t+1, head_2 predicts token t+2, and so on. - All these predictions happen simultaneously from the same point in the sequence, which is what provides the rich training signal.

metadata.section: How is it different than original MTP

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_How is it different than original MTP_1
text: - DeepSeek-V3 predicts two or more future tokens in this chained manner - Advantages - Because the model learns to anticipate more outcomes from a single context position, it gets more training signal per token seen - Empirical results in the paper show that multi-token prediction improves performance on generative tasks (e.g., code generation tasks) - ! (loss: /assets/images/paper/loss_for_mtp.png)

metadata.section: How is it different than original MTP

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_How is it different than original MTP_2
text: - All losses are accumulated, giving a denser total objective per position

metadata.section: How is it different than original MTP

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_0
text: Evidence?

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_1
text: Look for: - **Ablations** (does removing X hurt?) - **Costs** (not just accuracy) - **Stability** (loss spikes, divergence)

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_2
text: DeepSeek-V3 shows: - MTP improves downstream performance - MoE balancing stabilizes training - FP8 does not cause instability at scale

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_3
text: Every good paper has limits.

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_4
text: DeepSeek-V3:

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_5
text: - Requires massive infra (2048 H800s) - Custom kernels are non-trivial to reproduce - Deployment unit is still large - Inference speed ≠ solved forever

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_6
text: DeepSeek-V3 is an MoE Transformer that reduces active compute per token by routing tokens to a small subset of experts (37B activated vs 671B total). To make routing cheap and performant they (a) compress KV caches via Multi-Head Latent Attention (to shrink inference memory), (b) use a bias-driven routing update to balance expert load without a heavy auxiliary loss, and (c) densify supervision via Multi-Token Prediction (sequentially predicting D future tokens while preserving causal chains). On the infra side they push FP8 training (tile/block quantization + FP32 accumulation windows) and a pipeline scheme (DualPipe) to hide all-to-all communication — together those engineering choices let them claim strong benchmarks at a lower reported GPU cost

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_7
text: - MLA handles the memory/inference bottleneck. - MoE handles the compute/scaling bottleneck. - MTP provides a denser learning signal and further accelerates throughput

id: how to read a paper (Deepseekv3)_Summary_8
text: > If the model were a global shipping company, MLA is the advanced packaging that allows 90% more goods to fit in the same container; MoE is the specialized regional logistics centers that ensure only the necessary experts handle specific packages; and MTP is the predictive scheduling that allows the company to plan the next three stops of a delivery van at once instead of just one.

id: scaling laws_Question_0
text: What can LLMs do that classical ML can't? At scale, how do LLM's differ from traditional ML? What does this mean for the future of AI? Does more data mean better results? OpenAI wrote a paper just on this, it's called (**Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models**: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.08361)

id: scaling laws_Scaling Laws_6
text: *Questions we should ask ourselves:*

id: scaling laws_Scaling Laws_7
text: - Data vs performance (Are there simple rules that determine how data affects performance?) - Data vs model size (Do we train on more data or bigger models) - Hyper parameters vs performance (How should we set hyperparameter on big models)

id: scaling laws_Scaling Laws_8

id: scaling laws_Scaling Laws_9
text: This was the first idea of scaling laws in the 1970s^

id: scaling laws_Scaling Laws_10

id: scaling laws_Scaling Laws_16
text: - We have finite data, how does repeating examples affect scaling? - Upto 4 epochs repeating data is almost as good as new but after that it rapidly diminishing returns. - Given that repeated data is less valuable -> data selection should adapt to scale. - **Repeat high quality data OR include new data (trade-off)**

id: scaling laws_How can we design a huge LM? What to pick?_0
text: - **Architecture:** LSTM vs Transformer (Transformer loss decreases as we increase parameters (MOE is the only thing better than vanilla transformer)) - **Optimiser:** Adam is much better than SGD as we increase epochs (adaptive learning rate (basically takes steps automatically instead of a fixed size)) - **Depth:** layers >=6 is good, 1 vs 2 layers make huge difference after that we have plateud. - **Batch Size:** batch size increase -> gradient steps increase (past certain point -> diminishing returns (bias dominates instead of learning deeper features) - Critical BatchSize: minimum number of steps for target loss (compute increase -> steps can stay the same (BS fixed))
